#6630. Bond: The Business of James Bond

This week, the internet is abuzz with news of the much-anticipated casting of the new James Bond: Robert Pattinson, one of this year’s favorite leading men.

Pattinson’s arrival to the Bond franchise also marks the most luxury fashion-entrenched 007 actor yet. Pattinson has been a Dior ambassador for over 10 years, and has remained a key face for the brand since Jonathan Anderson took the helm in June last year. And in September — just two months before his Bond casting announcement — Pattinson was announced as Swiss watchmaker Jaeger-LeCoultre’s new global ambassador. The announcement generated $1 million in media impact value (MIV) within 48 hours for the brand, according to Launchmetrics.

Pattinson’s fashion affiliates were quick to stake their claim on the actor around the news of his casting. Dior’s Anderson posted an image of Pattinson and ex-Bond Daniel Craig on his personal Instagram story, taken at Anderson’s first Dior men’s 2026 show last summer, complete with a heart emoji. (Anderson had previously cast Craig in Loewe’s Fall/Winter 2024 campaign, around the same time he worked with the actor while doing the costumes for Luca Guadagnino’s Queer.) Richemont-owned Jaeger-LeCoultre, meanwhile, has posted two stills of the newly minted global ambassador to its Instagram account since Monday morning’s announcement.

Pattinson may have the most pre-existing off-screen deals of any Bond, but on-screen, the franchise is a blueprint for mega-deals between brands and movies. Partnerships have been part of the 007 world since Sean Connery stepped into the role of Bond in the inaugural Bond movie Dr. No in 1962, which featured hatmaker Lock & Co. Bond has driven an Aston Martin since 1964’s Goldfinger, Bollinger has been Bond’s champagne of choice since 1979’s Moonraker, and Heineken has been a partner since 1997. The beer brand has reportedly spent over $100 million on Bond sponsorship. Swiss watchmaker Omega is Bond’s longest-running sponsor and has decorated the wrists of Bonds since 1995, while also developing Bond watches for sale. (Prior to that, Bond wore a Rolex.) Past-era Bonds have cycled through different suit brands: Pierce Brosnan wore Brioni suits (and later starred in a campaign for the brand), as did Craig in Casino Royale. For the rest of Craig’s tenure, though, he wore Tom Ford.

The value of a Bond film has only grown. Spectre was estimated to feature $45 million in product placement; while the most recent Bond film — No Time to Die, Craig’s last — reportedly featured almost $100 million in brand placements and partnerships. In 2026, Bond’s on-screen value is immense. So much so that, last year, Amazon MGM Studios was said to have paid $20 million for the franchise, plus additional payouts that could total up to $1 billion to take full creative control over the franchise.

Brand deals have evolved dramatically since the early days of Bond — and even since the last movie. “Five years ago, an ambassadorship primarily meant red carpets and campaigns, while the film was kept separate,” says Krista Corrigan, senior retail analyst at EDITED. Now, they’re bleeding into the films themselves, whether by financially supporting films (and getting their clothes on-screen in the process), or inking deals with studios, as Dior recently did with A24. “Luxury brands give studios the aspirational quality that Bond depends on in return for a global marketing moment.”

Daniel Craig celebrating 60 years of James Bond in 2022.

The landscape into which this new Bond is releasing is dramatically different from the No Time to Die days of 2021. That was pre-Barbiecore, well before the number of brand-film-product collaborations for a given movie surpassed the hundreds, and was a different era of film promotion, before A24’s embrace of fashion and merch developed into a playbook in and of itself.

“What’s interesting about Bond is that there has always been that one iconic fashion moment or item everyone wants. Think Halle Berry’s orange bikini in Die Another Day,” says Adee Drexler, founder and CEO of communications agency ICA, who regularly brokers brand deals for clients. “These moments become part of pop culture and often live far beyond the film itself.”

The difference today, she argues, is that these moments can go viral overnight — which means the pressure to convert cultural relevance into commercial impact is heightened. “By aligning costume design, brand partnerships, and retail, the franchise can ensure that when an item captures the public’s attention, there’s already a way for consumers to buy into that moment,” Drexler says.

Will Pattinson’s be the most luxury-heavy Bond era yet? And how will the actor’s brand deals come into play?

Robert Pattinson in Dior for the Primetime screening in Venice.

Already, online chatter is bubbling about the impact of Pattinson’s current brand ambassadorships on the films. Puck’s Matt Belloni reported in his newsletter on Tuesday that Pattinson’s test deal didn’t address the actor’s current brand deals with Dior and Jaeger-LeCoultre, and that these will now need to be ironed out. One Redditor worried that Pattinson’s existing brand deals could delay filming. Most respondents expected not.

Still, it raises questions about how an actor’s off-screen brand ambassadorships influence their on-screen outfitting. “This is the first time in recent memory that a new Bond has been cast with a major luxury relationship already in place,” Corrigan says. “While brands have historically attached themselves to the role, this time it went to an actor already tied to Dior. With release expected in 2028, Dior —if involved — has plenty of time to design menswear around the film, which I’d expect to see over the next few seasons.”

Corrigan wouldn’t be surprised to see Dior on-screen come 2028, particularly given the brand’s recent embrace of the film industry and Anderson’s many costume designer credits. On November 12, Dior sent an email to US customers presenting Anderson’s cruise 2027 collection — shown in Los Angeles — as an exploration of the house’s Hollywood history, she notes.

Even if Dior isn’t integrated into the films themselves, the brand still stands to gain, Drexler says. “The press tour, premieres and cultural conversation create an enormous opportunity for Dior to own those fashion moments and translate that visibility into real commercial impact.”

Robert Pattinson in Dior, again, at the New York premiere of Die My Love.

Bond’s watch may be a different story. Jaeger-LeCoultre may have been posting Pattinson, but Omega wasted no time in staking its own claim on the Bond franchise. The brand got ahead of Pattinson’s casting by launching new models in its Seamaster diver’s watch collection, the James Bond and Spectre, in October. Omega will host an Art Basel Miami dinner to celebrate the Bond-themed timepieces. And on Tuesday morning, less than a day after Pattinson’s announcement, the watchmaker posted an image of its Seamaster Diver 300M James Bond Edition watch. Commenters were quick to pick up on what they expect to be a “battle” between the two Swiss watchmakers.

It may be a case of the highest bidder, and Omega is one of the largest watchmakers in the world (though Richemont CEO Johann Rupert recently told investors that Jaeger-LeCoultre was up 17% in the most recent quarter). Or it may be an on-screen, off-screen split. Some brand ambassadorship contracts include non-exclusivity clauses for filming. That said, when films know an actor is an ambassador for a given brand, producers will sometimes request to borrow clothing from that brand, given the existing relationship. For a moneyed franchise like Bond, though, no lending will be necessary. Instead, it’s a question of which brand will be Pattinson’s official outfitter.

Plus, for a role like Bond, the character the actor plays on-screen does become synonymous with the actor off-screen, particularly given how long the actor remains in the role. (Pattinson has a three-film deal.) One couldn’t imagine Craig donning Omega watches on-screen, while shilling non-Omega watches off-screen. In fact, the actor was — and still is — an official Omega ambassador.

Whichever brands do fill out this next iteration of the Bond world, they’ll have even more work cut out for them than in eras past, Drexler says. “It’s about moving beyond traditional product placement and creating partnerships that can capitalize on cultural moments in real time, without compromising the authenticity of the Bond universe.”

#6628. Drinking Tea Too Hot Could Be Bad For Your Health—Here's What To Know

Your morning cup might benefit from a little patience.

There’s more than one reason to brew your tea at the right temperature—and one of those reasons could affect your health. A recently published study followed nearly half a million adults in China for almost a decade, examining how tea-drinking habits related to their health. Researchers found that regular tea drinkers had a lower risk of vascular disease than non-tea drinkers. But one major caveat emerged: Those who reported drinking their tea “burning hot” had a higher risk of vascular disease.

According to the study, drinking extremely hot tea was associated with a 16 percent higher relative risk of vascular disease. But don't give up your daily tea habit quite yet. “This study is interesting, but we don't have a proven biological explanation yet,” Dr. Niraj Patel, medical director at Clara, says.

Dr. Chelsea Azarcon is similarly cautious about drawing conclusions from the findings.

“It doesn’t look like this study has any proposed mechanism for why burning hot tea would increase the risk of cardiovascular disease,” she explains. “However, we do know that drinks that are too hot can increase the risk of esophageal cancer by creating local injury and damage.”

That concern is supported by the World Health Organization's cancer research agency, which has classified drinking beverages hotter than 149°F as probably carcinogenic to humans. The classification specifically concerns esophageal cancer, though, so it doesn't explain the connection to vascular disease identified in the new study.

The study didn’t identify a specific temperature at which drinking tea becomes detrimental to vascular health. And although researchers found an association between drinking extremely hot tea and vascular disease, that doesn't necessarily mean one causes the other.

ScienceDaily also notes that drinking tea at extremely high temperatures may diminish some of the health benefits associated with regular tea consumption.

Azarcon believes further research into tea's chemical makeup and how it may change at different temperatures could help answer some of the remaining questions.

"I'd say enjoy your tea, but don't feel like you need to drink it while it's scalding hot,” Patel suggests. “There's a difference between brewing tea with hot water and actually drinking it at that temperature. Letting it cool for a few minutes is an easy precaution and doesn't require giving up something you enjoy."

So while I don’t plan on giving up my tea habit any time soon, I am definitely making extra sure that I let my cup sit out a little longer before taking that first sip.

#6621. The Cutest Way to Wear Your Short Hair Right Now? A Flipped Bob.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

What’s one thing Ariana Grande and Hailey Bieber have in common right now? Their flipped bobs. (Bobiana Grande, anyone?) Bobs in all forms have basically taken over the hair world, from French bobs and Italian bobs to blunt bobs and bell-bottom bobs. I would’ve guessed, at this point, that bobs had bobbed their last bob. Alas, another one has appeared: the flipped bob. (At this point, there are probably almost as many types of bobs as times I’ve said “bob” in this paragraph. Anyway.)

Inspired by the voluminous, flipped-out hairstyles of the 1960s, the fun, bouncy finish on this retro look is super chic. Plus, they’re so in for this time of year: “Flipped bobs are very trendy for the holiday season and a perfect style for holiday parties,” says celebrity hairstylist Nicolas Flores. And the best part? If you already have a bob, you don’t necessarily need a new haircut to get in on the trend. A blow-dryer-and-brush combo or flat iron can do the trick to give your existing bob that sought-after flick. Looking for some flipped bob ideas? Ahead, some expert tips from Flores on getting the look and plenty of inspo pics to reference before you start styling.

A flipped bob is just a classic bob haircut, but with one very important twist: The ends are styled outward rather than straight or curled in. It “focuses more on curling the ends outward and away from the face, giving a fun, flirty look,” says Flores. The result? A playful, totally-bouncy hairstyle that was made popular in the ‘60s by beauty icons like Jackie Kennedy and Mary Tyler Moore and is now being worn by some of today’s beauty icons like Grande and Bieber.

While the original flipped bob had a ton of volume and serious outward curl, the current versions we’re seeing are a little more subtle, sleek, and versatile, sometimes just barely flicked away from your face. The style works well on all lengths of bobs, from chin-grazing cuts to longer, shoulder-length lobs. You can also customize them with bangs, layers, a side part, or however you normally like to wear your bob.

Before any styling happens, think about your haircut. If you already have a bob, you don’t need to worry about cutting it shorter or anything like that. But if you’re getting a bob for the first time with the intention of styling it with the ends flipped out, “tell your stylist you don’t want to go too short,” says Flores, since the styling can make the hair look even shorter. “I always recommend an inch-and-a-half to two inches below the hairline to get that perfect length,” he says.

“I’d start with damp hair, a little volumizing mousse, and some heat protectant,” he says. The Cosmo Holy Grail Beauty Award-winning Nexxus Hy-Volume Weightless Lift Cloud Foam and Roz Air Thickening Spray are two great options. Section your hair and apply two to three pumps of each product at your roots, working it through to the ends.

“Using a medium round brush, blow dry the hair nice and smooth, giving it a little lift at the roots,” says Flores.

Don’t forget to focus on the star of the show: those flippy ends. “Once you get to the ends, turn the brush upward and away from the neck to create that cute little flip,” says Flores. “Give it a quick blast of cool air before releasing the brush so it holds its shape.” That’ll give a more natural-looking flip, but for something more dramatic, reach for a flat iron after you finish the blowout. “If you want the flip to be a little more defined, you can go back in with a flat iron and gently flick the ends outward,” adds Flores. “Just a little turn of the wrist is all you need!”

After that, you’re pretty much at the finish line: “Finish with a light hairspray to keep everything in place without making it stiff,” says Flores. “The goal is to keep the bob looking soft, bouncy, and effortless.” Spritz it lightly all over, but focus on the ends especially to keep that flippy look in place all day.

Now that you know how to style a flipped bob, check out these flipped bob ideas so you can recreate the fun look for yourself.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmo. She’s written about all things hair, from cool hair color trends to the best haircuts worth trying.

#6620. Anne Hathaway Gives Birth to Her Third Child

Congratulations are in order for Anne Hathaway! The actor has welcomed her third child with husband Adam Shulman, making them a family of five.

On Tuesday, November 17, Hathaway was photographed out and about in New York City with a newborn nestled against her chest in a baby carrier. People has since independently confirmed the happy news. The baby’s name, sex, and exact birth date have not yet been shared.

Hathaway and Shulman, who married in 2012, are already parents to two boys: Jonathan, 10, and Jack, who was born in November 2019. The couple have largely kept their children out of the public eye.

The Oscar winner first announced her third pregnancy in June, with a sweet Instagram video soundtracked by Barbara Lewis’s “Baby I’m Yours.” Wearing a flowing white linen two-piece by Nothing Fits But and gold-embellished Cult Gaia sandals, Hathaway walked into the frame, revealed her growing bump, beamed at the camera, and ran playfully out of sight. “x Baby, I’m yours x,” she captioned the post. During an appearance on Late Night With Seth Meyers the following month, she affectionately referred to the surprise addition as the couple’s “buzzer-beater” baby.

It’s been a pregnancy style journey for Annie. Working with stylist Erin Walsh, Hathaway delivered some of the year’s most memorable maternity looks: goddess-like custom Dior and Prada gowns on The Odyssey press tour, as well as more playful, bump-baring separates, and an ethereal lilac Alexander McQueen dress during New York Fashion Week. She rounded out her run of red carpets at the Verity premiere in September, wearing a dramatic black sequined tulle Prabal Gurung gown.

Indeed, if anyone has earned a little downtime, it’s Anne Hathaway. The actor has had an extraordinarily busy 2026, with five films released this year alone: Mother Mary, The Devil Wears Prada 2, The Odyssey, The End of Oak Street, and Verity. Between reprising her beloved role as Andy Sachs, playing Penelope in Christopher Nolan’s Greek epic, and diving deep into Colleen Hoover’s much hyped psychological thriller, Hathaway has scarcely stopped the promo tour.

But now, she’s looking forward to some time away from the spotlight. Speaking to Vogue at the Verity premiere, Hathaway shared that her favorite moment of the entire year had been discovering she was pregnant, and the forthcoming opportunity to take a pause. “I’m really excited to meet my baby, and to be in that little bubble in time,” she said.

Five films plus a fabulous maternity wardrobe, and a new baby. Congratulations once again to Anne Hathaway and Adam Schulman!

#6619. The Best Coffee-Table Books to Gift Your Beautiful, Discerning Friends

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

These books will please everyone on your gift list this year

Every year holidays come around, and a slight panic sets in at the thought of finding gifts that the people you love will get excited about—and that will make them feel seen. The real trick is to keep a list throughout the year of everything you see that reminds you of this person or that person. But because sometimes you don’t write things down because you’re “sure you’ll remember,” and because even if you do, we need all the help we can get in discovering cool things, we’ve put together a list of our favorite coffee-table books to give (and to receive, if we’re being honest) this year.

From fashion monographs to punk rock album covers to a guide to medieval wellness, we promise that we’ve found something that will thrill even your most cynical friend.

Richard Avedon was undoubtedly one of the greatest photographers of the 20th century and this collection gathers his work for Harper’s Bazaar from 1944 to 1965. As the world experienced generation-defining shifts, Avedon was zeroed in on his style, creating indelible images that would go on to change fashion. Bonus? It pairs perfectly with Ron Howard’s documentary on the photographer, also titled simply Avedon.

This massive pink tome, assembled by Coppola herself from her own collection of photographs, scripts, collages, and all manner of feminine detritus, offers a revealing and inspirational look at the director’s process and world-building.

With wit and humor, medievalist Larisa Grollemond sheds light on the way humans lived—and thrived(?)—during the middle ages. Is it true they never bathed? Did they have practice birth control? Were witches in fact, doctors? This books holds the answers.

Raymond Pettibon may now be a certified blue-chip artist, but he began his career in the 1970s drawing flyers and record covers for punk bands in Southen California like Minutemen and Black Flag. (He also designed their iconic four-bar logo, which has now been meme-fied.) This book collects his musical body of work, which also includes the Foo Fighters and Lana del Rey—that’s his work on the cover of Norman Fucking Rockwell.

The elusive Martin Margiela may very well be the designer that has most influenced contemporary fashion. Nowhere is that more evident than in this book that looks at the time when the Belgian designer was at the helm of Hermés. The enduring appeal of the collections he created from 1997 to 2002 would go on to set the tone for the whole quiet luxury moment we’ve been living under—except better.

Jeff Goodwin was the makeup artist for David Lynch’s iconic film Blue Velvet. His personal trove of Polaroid photos capture impromptu behind-the-scenes moments and reveal how he refined the makeup looks; they’re accompanied by his own memories of the filming experience.

How many people’s fashion obsessions began as they endlessly dressed and undressed their dolls—be they Barbie, Bratz, or even American Girl dolls? This tome looks at the symbiotic relationship between dolls and real-life grown-up fashion, zeroing in on the works of designers like Comme des Garçons’ Rei Kawakubo and Viktor & Rolf’s Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren, among others.

This is a book designed to inspire. For “Kitchen Piece,” Ono suggests one “hangs a canvas on a wall” and “throws all the leftovers you have” on it, with the caveat that “you may prepare special food for the piece.” After spending time with Ono’s instructions, one realizes there is art to be found literally everywhere.

This is the only book about Carolyn Bessette Kennedy that one may ever need. Sunita Kumar Nair talks to CBK’s friends and, through a carefully curated edit of images, breaks down her style. She also reveals the true essence of the person behind all those infinitely rebloggable images.

Past Continuous is the name of an exhibit at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York that brings together the world of Lee Krasner and her husband Jackson Pollock and looks at their career arcs in tandem. It begins with a selection of their paintings before the pair met, and traces their influences, taking a closer look at how their presences wove in and out of each other’s work.

This tome celebrates America’s 250th anniversary through over 200 pages filled with iconic images that have defined the country throughout its history, from images of cowboys wearing their worn-in Levi’s and immigrants landing at Ellis Island to Martin Luther King and Elvis Presley.

Diane Arbus’s unflinching photographs captured humanity in all its beautiful and exacting rawness. Documents tells the history of her short-lived career through essays, criticism, and other ephemera from 1967 through the present day; it’s a comprehensive guide to understanding her work.

Glen Luchford photographed a few of Prada’s most iconic ad campaigns of the 1990s. This book brings them all together along with alternate shots and test shots, and is an essential for both Prada aficionados and lovers of the decade.

Created in 1909 by Arthur E. Waite and Pamela Colman Smith in London, the appropriately titled Waite Smith tarot deck is the most popular deck in the world. This book looks at its history, uncovering the details and meaning of each individual card—and it comes with its own set of cards.

This year, the Fashion Museum Antwerp is celebrating its 40th anniversary with an exhibition dedicated to the “Antwerp Six,” the name the fashion media gave to a group of designers—Dries van Noten, Ann Demeulemeeter, Marina Yee, Dirk Bikkembergs, Walter Van Beirendonck, and Dirk Van Seene—that arrived in London in the mid ’80s fresh after their graduation from the Royal Academy of Fine Art. For those who can’t make it to Belgium to see the show, the book may prove to be the next best thing, chock full of photographs, illustrations, newspaper clippings, and essays. They may not have all become household names, but their influence can still be felt on the runways today.

Brianna Capozzi’s unique view of womanhood has made her one of the most sought-after photographers in fashion. Her latest monograph features a mix of magazine shots of famous singers and actors with images of impromptu shoots staged with her best friends. The result is a visual shot of adrenaline and a reminder that girls—well, women—just wanna have fun!

#6618. 5 Restaurant Chains With Troubling Food Safety Records

Let's just say the health department had a few notes.

Not every day can be a home-cooked meal kind of day. Sometimes, going out really pays off. It saves you time in the kitchen, cuts down on effort, and most importantly, lets you relax while someone else does the heavy lifting. Many families turn to fast food when they want an easy, quick meal or when time is of the essence. But where you go can really make a difference.

Admittedly, fast food chains don’t always have the best reputation, especially when it comes to health concerns. But beyond the macros, another factor to consider is cleanliness.

Cleaning protocols differ from chain to chain—and even from location to location. You may have seen headlines concerning less-than-stellar hygiene reports stemming from certain fast food locations over the years. Kitchen cleanliness is paramount to food safety (just look at this year’s Cyclospora outbreak), and some chains have faced more than their share of troubling headlines. Here are five fast food chains with a disappointing history of food safety issues.

I hate to break it to burrito-with-extra-guac fans, but Chipotle has a history of high-profile food safety issues. The company paid $25 million to resolve criminal charges related to a series of foodborne illness outbreaks between 2015 and 2018. According to the documents, Chipotle was charged with "adulterating food in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act," resulting in the largest criminal fine ever imposed in a food safety case at the time.

Records cited at least five foodborne illness outbreaks across several states, including incidents involving norovirus, that sickened more than 1,100 people. These outbreaks "primarily stemmed from store-level employees' failure to follow company food safety protocols." Personally, I'd rather have a side of hot sauce than a side of stomach flu.

In February 2025, a Massachusetts store was cited for nine core health code violations—including insufficiently cleaned ice machines, improperly stored produce, and missing thermometers in a walk-in cooler—along with one priority foundation violation. Such issues can raise concerns about food safety and sanitation.

In 2022, a health inspector described another location in the state as "very unclean." A year before that, workers at a Springfield, Missouri, location staged a walkout over poor working conditions. A subsequent health inspection found that "the floors in the food preparation area (especially under equipment and near drains), walk-in refrigerator and freezer, and dry storage areas were not clean," leading to a follow-up inspection. (Don't even get us started on some of the issues found overseas!)

Sorry, chalupa lovers. Taco Bell has also faced its share of food safety concerns over the years. Reports include an E. coli outbreak along the East Coast in 2006 resulting in 71 illnesses (53 of whom were hospitalized), two Salmonella outbreaks in 2010 affecting at least 155 people across 21 states, and a hepatitis A outbreak in 2000 that sickened 23 people and hospitalized 15.

More recently, a customer’s viral video appeared to show a Taco Bell kitchen strewn with food, garbage, and old boxes near food prep areas. Some commenters suggested that it was filmed during rush hour while the restaurant was understaffed and that employees were too busy to clean. Still, it's not a great look for in-store hygiene.

Big Mac lovers, look away. The Golden Arches have faced numerous lawsuits over food safety issues over the years, including a class action suit (plus several personal injury suits) filed in 2024 following a multistate E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounders. The outbreak ultimately sickened 104 people and killed one, with investigators identifying slivered onions as the likely source of contamination.

The Boston City Department of Inspectional Services found nearly 125 violations at seven different McDonald's locations between 2018 and 2019—everything from mismanaged storage to mold, rat droppings, and even live cockroaches. Complaints and lawsuits have also alleged undercooked meat and foodborne illnesses caused by cross-contamination.

Wendy's locations have racked up numerous health code violations, too (one Las Vegas restaurant in particular drew 27 demerits in a 2019 inspection for dirty soda nozzles, food left on the floor, raw food cross-contamination, and more). A 2023 "Dirty Dining" segment called out a Fort Lauderdale, Florida, location with an inspection that found insects all over the restaurant.

Perhaps most concerningly, a Michigan family filed a lawsuit in 2024 alleging their daughter developed hemolytic uremic syndrome following an E. coli infection they attributed to food from Wendy's. According to the lawsuit, the illness caused permanent brain damage, kidney failure, a seizure disorder, and other lasting health problems. Inspectors had found the location in violation of 17 different health and food codes just days before the family's visit, including moldy food, spoiled produce, dirty surfaces, and water leaks.

Even with these histories of violations, not every location should make you rethink your dining options—many restaurants are up to code and clean. While all this information is enough to convince me to stick to home-cooked meals for the rest of my life, I suggest checking your local restaurant's latest health inspection report before deciding whether or not to visit your chain of choice.

#6615. Hunter Schafer’s Peekaboo Ponytail Is the Cool Girl’s Red Carpet Look

From intricate braids and gravity-defying knots to elaborate, architectural chignons, the red carpet has seen plenty of sculptural hair looks as of late. Leave it to Hunter Schafer to offer a decidedly cool-girl interpretation of the trend.

Attending the London premiere of Blade Runner 2099 on Tuesday evening, Schafer—styled as always by Dara—wore a custom ivory Celine ensemble comprising a strapless satin bustier dress, with a dramatic train trailing behind her, layered over tailored tuxedo trousers for that nonchalant elegance. Her beauty followed suit. Working with her go-to hairstylist Rena Calhoun, Schafer wore her honey-blonde lengths in softly tousled, loose waves, parted loosely at the center and falling around her shoulders. From the front it was a classic and romantic, and a rather effortless-looking hairstyle. But turn around, and there was a delightful little surprise: a tiny, twisted, extremely low ponytail woven into the ends of her hair at the nape of her neck, secured with a wrap of blonde strands. The mini braid was a lovely, blink-and-you’ll-miss-it detail. Makeup artist Sandy Ganzer kept things similarly soft, with subtly defined eyes, flushed cheeks, and a rosy pink lip.

It’s another clever beauty moment in what’s proving to be an excellent press tour for Schafer. At the Los Angeles premiere last week, Ganzer paid homage to Daryl Hannah’s replicant character Pris in Ridley Scott’s original Blade Runner, creating a dramatic, futuristic strip of gunmetal eyeshadow across her eyes and nose. Calhoun fashioned her hair into a disheveled updo, with flyaways escaping at the back for a cyberpunk heroine to red carpet look.

Then there were the hair-matching fuzzy earmuffs from Undercover’s fall 2007 collection, which Calhoun incorporated into a double-ponytail hairstyle. Working alongside Dara and Ganzer, Schafer has been having enormous fun with beauty references that are both deeply considered and playful, often drawing on the sci-fi world of her forthcoming series and beyond.

The up-do renaissance is firmly upon us. At this year’s Golden Globes, Audrey Nuna, Mia Goth, and Jenna Ortega were among those experimenting with interesting shapes and structures, while Anya Taylor-Joy recently sported a sleek knot at the LACMA Art+Film Gala.

What’s so great about Hunter Schafer’s latest look is its restraint. While everyone else is twisting, sculpting, and shellacking their hair into elaborate works of art, Schafer makes a case for something more low-key. Sometimes the most interesting beauty detail is the one you almost miss.

#6613. Inde Navarrette Credits Actresses Who Gave Her ‘Permission to Be Free’

For ELLE Women in Hollywood honoree Inde Navarrette, playing Nikki in Obsession was about far more than landing her first leading role. In her acceptance speech at our annual event at the Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles at Beverly Hills last night, the actress spoke about putting everything that she had into playing the character. “I needed to break through every glass ceiling either school, peers, society, or even I put on myself,” she said. “I needed to be connected with that rage that I used to find solace in. I needed to be reminded that my voice, whether soft or loud, holds weight and creates tension that I get to be in control of. I can play a girl who has an internal world—crazy!—whom is the lead of a film and whom is not the perfect victim. Nikki was my opportunity to show the world what I knew I could do and to that, I have to say thank you.”

She went on to thank Obsession’s writer and director Curry Barker, along with all actresses who inspired her early on (including Bryce Dallas Howard, who presented Navarrette with the award). “Thank you not only to Curry Barker for writing a role that allowed me that chance, but thank you to all of the women that took that chance before me,” she said. “Thank you to Jessica Lange for showing me and all of her work that there is beauty in madness and to just give it to the world. Thank you to Natalie Portman for Léon: The Professional. It was the first time I got to see a kid in a movie being more than a kid. She was me. Thank you to Sally Field and Steel Magnolias for daring to portray grief honestly and the hardships of motherhood gracefully. Thank you, Bryce Dallas Howard and The Help, for portraying how intersectional womanhood can divide us and that women who look different than ourselves are no different than ourselves. Thank you to Florence Pugh, Carrie Coon, Julianne Moore, Elizabeth Debicki, Samantha Morton, Rosalind Eleazar, Penélope Cruz. Thank you for daring to be wild. Thank you. Incredibly, you have all given me permission to be free. Let’s all shine a light in each other.”

#6612. How to Maintain Long, Healthy Hair Over 50, According to Experts

From top treatments to when to plan your next trim, here’s everything to know

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There’s something undeniably chic about a head of long, luscious hair. Think glossy, waist-skimming, bouncy, voluminous lengths that make extensions an option rather than a long-term commitment. What’s more, long hair provides the ultimate canvas for experimentation, with styling possibilities that feel limitless.

As hair matures, however, maintaining the same level of shine, strength, and vitality can require more attention. As texture changes and dryness increases, the key is to adapt your routine to give your longer lengths the care they deserve. “Long hair can look beautiful at any age, but keeping mature hair glossy and healthy-looking is all about replenishing moisture and maintaining shine,” says celebrity hairstylist Naomi Brooks. “I always recommend prioritising hydrating products that help smooth the hair cuticle, improve softness, and enhance shine, alongside regular trims to keep the lengths and ends looking healthy.”

If you’re considering making the transition and letting your bob grow out, look to a host of celebrities for inspiration. From Demi Moore and Naomi Campbell to Andie MacDowell and Claudia Schiffer, countless iterations are proving just how effortless long hair can look on women over 50. As Brooks explains: “Demi Moore is a fantastic example of how beautiful long hair can look at any age. Her hair is consistently glossy, healthy-looking, and full of movement.”

While genetics certainly play a role, Moore’s glossy lengths are also the result of great care and strategic products. Her hairstylist, Dimitris Giannetos, revealed on social media that he often relies on Kérastase’s Gloss Absolu Glaze Drops Anti-Frizz Hair Oil to reduce frizz, boost shine, and ensure hair remains sleek without looking too heavy. Indeed, experts recommend investing in a high-quality hydrating treatment to ensure mature hair is treated with extra care. “Mature hair can become drier, finer or more fragile over time, so maintaining moisture and shine is important,” says Warren Edwards, creative director at Warren & the Hare.

Additionally, for those with gray or silver hair, session stylist Danilo Giangreco recommends incorporating a clear gloss into your routine to enhance shine. This can also help counteract any unwanted brassiness, ensuring hair appears brighter and healthier.

Another expert-approved tip is to keep heat styling to a minimum where possible. If you do rely on hot tools, applying heat protectant can help shield strands from damage while preserving moisture, strength, and shine.

Finally, contrary to popular belief, long hair thrives on regular maintenance. Though it may seem counterintuitive when trying to grow your hair, routine appointments are essential to keep split ends at bay and prevent the ends from looking too thin or tired. In turn, this helps keep long, mature hair looking fuller, healthier, and overall more glossy.

#6611. The 15 Best Airbnbs in the Alps, Whether You’re an Avid Skier or Just in it for the Après

We are headed right into the thick of ski season; when warm, wool knitwear is the uniform du jour, and the temperature is the kind of cold that’s completely inexcusable unless accompanied by plates of melty raclette at après-ski. This is your sign to book your winter getaway in advance. And while there are tons of great ski resorts you could jet off to, nothing quite beats an Alpine retreat—whether freeskiing in Zermatt or trialing bunny slopes in Megève, you have options. The best Airbnbs in the Alps, from Austria to France to Italy, are the perfect place to stay if you need more flexibility and space than a hotel.

It’s a vast region—the Dolomites alone are an 18-peak range—so there’s a lot to choose from. Go for stately chalet elegance with a multi-bedroom option if you’re traveling with lots of friends and family; book something closer to a cozy cabin if you prefer a low-key holiday. These 15 options span the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps, as well as a range of prices and styles. Your next decision? Which Fair Isle sweater will make it into your carry-on.

Those in search of the most traditional of Alpine vacations will find everything they’re looking for in this peaceful chalet—right down to the Savoyard pottery. It looks out onto the Aravis mountains, just five minutes away from the Croix-Fry ski resort and 40 minutes from the busier spots of Annecy and Megève. It has a wood-burning fireplace that’s ideal for relaxing after a day on the slopes, and a spacious balcony for those brave enough to wrap up and take their coffee outdoors in the winter chill.

Situate yourself in the heart of one of the most sought-after ski resorts, close to all of Gstaad’s main shops. The apartment, which can sleep up to six, has heated underground parking and a ski cellar to facilitate winter trips. The interior is simple but well-appointed—the dining table being a major plus for cozy dinners—but the real draw is the balcony. Head outside for gorgeous mountain views whenever you want them.

If you’re not looking for a fully remote stay, this charming mini-chalet gives you a taste of quaint mountain village life. Renovated in 2024, the updated amenities list includes a pizza stone oven, walk-in shower, and hypoallergenic bedding. (Your booking also comes with a Beatenberg guest card, a perk inclusive of a free bus pass for travel back and forth to Interlaken for when you want to explore the alpine area.) This has all the cozy touches you’ll want for a weeklong vacation, plus one important extra: The wraparound balcony has storybook views of both Lake Thun and the Eiger, Mönch, and Jungfrau peaks.

Not all alpine retreats are stuffy, rustic cabins; some are luxurious, light-filled homes that expertly blend old and new. This spot is a perfect example. The 18th-century farmhouse right in the historic center square of Scuol was recently restored, keeping its old-world charms (that wood paneling!) while making some necessary updates. Sleek chrome furniture, a chef-grade kitchen, and whitewashed walls bring light in.

There’s no television in this mountainside cabin; all the better to truly unwind with. Instead, occupy yourself with a forest hike or a day on the slopes (the Airbnb is in the La Tzoumaz resort, by Verbier in the Swiss Alps). Wind down by candlelight, whether that’s with a warm meal served family-style at the dining table overlooking the tall trees or a game of Hearts by the fire.

It’s pretty hard to beat these views. This restored barn looks out onto Mount Pelmo in the Dolomites, with a key highlight being the covered balcony; you’ll want to take every meal there to soak in the mountain views. It can fit up to seven guests—great for a large family or group—and you’ll each have plenty of space to stretch out in.

This charming cottage in the Valais town of Ayer puts you right near all the top ski resorts: Grimentz, Zinal, St-Luc, and Chandolin are all about a 15-minute drive away. The combined dining-living space is charming, with windows that look out onto snowy hills in the winter and green pastures (plus the occasional cow) in the summer. Four bedrooms offers plenty of space for a big friend trip.

From the outside, surrounded by snowy pine trees, this chalet looks like a fairytale cottage; inside, it’s outfitted with all the contemporary amenities to make your stay a luxurious one. A Bose Bluetooth sound system, HDTV with all the streamers, and state-of-the-art kitchen appliances bring a modern element to the wood cabin. A private sauna and hot tub only add to the five-star feel.

It’s an easy drive to the alpine lake and mountains of the Salzkammergut region from this Airbnb, which sits on a spacious property surrounded by forest. Sweat out the day in the sauna or gather around the fireplace to listen to a vinyl or play a board game—both are provided by the host.

With Montblanc in the distance, this 19th-century cottage offers picturesque views from the balcony. Take your morning coffee there before heading out to the slopes or nearby hiking trails, returning home to soak in the tub, whip up a home-cooked meal, or crack open a new book in the glass-walled (and, crucially, heated) reading room.

Expect charm at every turn with this farmhouse, which dates back to the 15th century. Located in the Kaiser Mountains of the Eastern Alps, this sprawling property features wooden ceilings, terracotta tiled floors (with partial underfloor heating), and beautiful murals painted throughout—there’s even an original stove in the dining room.

This rustic mountain hut located in a secluded part of the Italian alps is actually a working farm and apiary: Those with a fear of bees, plan accordingly. A breakfast basket is provided each morning, with the freshest of ingredients you can enjoy outdoors or in the open-air kitchen in the warmer months, or by the fire in the winter. You’ll need a car to access the property—it is properly remote—but its isolation is part of the charm.

This French Alps home is ideally built for family holidays. Child-friendly features, from a travel crib to fireplace grates, will make your stay more comfortable; several separate bathrooms give everyone their own space; upscale amenities, like heated flooring and optional catering, make every day feel like a treat. It’s just south of Lake Geneva, if you want to rent a car and take a little day trip.

This apartment in the Dolomites is deceptively spacious: It sleeps up to six, with soaring A-frame ceilings giving the illusion of even more space. The theme appears to be, simply, wood. From the exposed beams to the built-in furniture to the floor-to-ceiling cupboards, the whole space is designed with rustic cabins on the brain.

#6610. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Party Brought Everyone Out

There’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, with special thanks to the 1 Hotel West Hollywood.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

Midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. Garfield’s forthcoming Artificial (out December 25) is the movie on everybody’s lips, but he told me he’s looking forward to spending the holidays in New York and taking a brief break before what will probably be a busy campaign season for the Man of the Year.

No one captured the evening as succinctly as Robby Hoffman, who described her upcoming TV show as “Curb [Your Enthusiasm] for poor people.” When the conversation turned back to GQ, Hoffman rued the decline of magazine paper quality. But this latest issue got her seal of approval: appropriately glossy, well-considered, and elite to the touch. Though she might have just been describing the party’s guest list.

But even if you didn’t make the cut, you can see how GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party looked from the inside. ✦

It’s hard to believe it’s been nearly a decade and a half since Jennifer Lawrence first stepped into the career-defining role of Katniss Everdeen—bringing Suzanne Collins’s Hunger Games trilogy to life with a 2012 film adaptation. Alongside costars Josh Hutcherson (who played Peeta Mellark) and Liam Hemsworth (Gale Hawthorne), the actor spent her early twenties on and off the dystopian set, subsequently filming the 2013 sequel, Hunger Games: Catching Fire, and the two-part Mockingjay finale, released in 2014 and 2015. #6607. Carrie Coon Speaks Out About Women’s Representation at ELLE’s Women in Hollywood Event

Carrie Coon had a question for her fellow Women in Hollywood honorees: “Can we start a studio?”

On Monday night, the actress took the stage at ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood celebration in Los Angeles, where she called for women in the entertainment industry to come together and create more opportunities for themselves.

Coon was introduced by her Gilded Age co-star Louisa Jacobson, who celebrated her recent career achievements.

“Carrie is a crusader, always fighting tirelessly for artistic integrity in a landscape that seems to value high gloss and profit over honest, nuanced storytelling,” Jacobson said. “And if you know Carrie, you know that she is completely allergic to superficiality.”

In her acceptance speech, Coon reflected on the importance of women’s stories, drawing inspiration from feminist literature and End Times Fascism, a book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor.

“Patriarchy, capitalism...these are hierarchical systems of domination that rely on fear,” she said. “And in this paradigm, women and girls, like our natural resources, are a disposable commodity—and as such, according to philosopher Kate Manne—our stories are interchangeable and of equal power. But of course, they’re not. That’s not true. And we’re not a monolith.”

Coon went on to discuss the performances of her fellow honorees, arguing that their work represented something extraordinary. “In these women, I see the fight for the living world. I see moral clarity. I see imagination. I see courage,” she said. “And these are, in fact, the antidotes to fascism. That’s how important this storytelling is.”

Toward the end of her speech, Coon questioned how women in Hollywood could create lasting change beyond events celebrating their individual achievements.

“How do we forge our collective safety and solidarity in an ethic of communalism?” she asked. “Okay, so this is the part of the speech where I don’t actually have the answer to that question, but I make the appeal that nights like these shouldn’t be one-off nights.”

She concluded with the aforementioned proposition for her peers: “And so I’m going to start with a really stupid question, but I’m not afraid to ask a stupid question: Can we start a studio?”

#6606. The 15 Best Airbnbs in Tokyo for an Authentic Japanese Experience

It’s no secret that Japan has perfected the art of, well, a lot of things—design, cuisine, wellness, hospitality, and craft, to name a few. A trip to Japan offers a glimpse at living with intention and elegant restraint, from the traditional tea ceremonies to the ritual of long soaks in an onsen. In its populous capital, slowing down might feel like a contradiction, but the best Airbnbs in Tokyo offer travelers respite from the bustle.

Winter is an especially beautiful time to visit. The crowds thin out and the city is illuminated by trees glowing with little white lights—it feels like your own personal winter wonderland. Those visiting around New Year’s celebrations, or Shōgatsu, can participate in a long list of traditions, from visiting temples and shrines to eating a bowl of buckwheat noodles in warm broth, to ensure luck for the year ahead. Whether you’re looking to explore Shinjuku’s narrow alleys lined with tiny bars or prefer to spend your time in Shimokitazawa’s bohemian district amidst the cafes and vintage shops, these Airbnb rentals will situate you in Tokyo’s most compelling neighborhoods.

This design-forward spot starts with a lofty living room and just gets better. Recently renovated in August 2026, the unique property used to be a sign shop before it was converted into an inviting vacation rental. From the exposed wood beams to the rustic pottery that lines nearly every available surface, it’s a perfect reflection of the city’s creative energy. It also fits up to 10 guests; if your trip to Tokyo is part of a big group holiday, this is the place to book.

Slightly more modern-minimalist than traditional, this two-story home is the perfect longer stay for a family (it sleeps up to six). The quiet neighborhood includes a park, a nice bit of green respite for those traveling with children, and it’s well-located for exploring. Natural materials and muted colors create quite the calming spot—though hints of playfulness, like a fish decal in the bathroom, ensure it’s not devoid of personality.

Ideal for larger groups, this four-bedroom home offers a serene spot of respite in the city, complete with a zen garden, a rooftop terrace, and a soaking tub. Its residential neighborhood is equally as tranquil, and here, you’re just a walk away from some of Tokyo’s expansive green spaces like the Meiji Jingu Shrine Garden and the Akasaka Palace and its gardens. (For those craving something livelier, the National Stadium Plaza is not far away.)

Amenities: Balcony, bathtub, washer and dryer

With sculptural lighting, sleek, angular furnishings, and a small collection of contemporary art all contributing to a moody tone, this three-bedroom apartment feels subtly seductive. A traditional painted screen provides an exquisite counterpoint to the apartment’s otherwise decidedly modern interiors. Its location puts some of the city's most significant sights, such as the Tokyo Skytree and the Sensoji Temple, within easy walking distance; if it’s your first time in the city, this is a convenient home base.

Amenities: Elevator, balcony, bathtub, washer, AC

Clean lines, a restrained palette, and geometric motifs await in this elegantly pared-back house, which feels more minimalist case study than typical vacation rental. Located in the residential neighborhood of Nakano, the three-story home offers a sense of stillness amidst the city’s constant motion. With three bedrooms and three bathrooms, there’s ample room for groups to settle in. The interiors are elegantly pared back, reflecting the timelessness of Japanese design, and the oversized square tub makes for the perfect antidote to a long day exploring the city or browsing the shops of nearby Nakano Broadway.

Amenities: Air conditioning, bathtub, washer, TV, hot tub, free parking, cleaning available during stay

This earth-toned home occupies a three-story standalone building that’s located a few minutes from the Sagenjaya Station (and just 10 minutes by train to Shibuya). The interiors are serene and softly lit, and include amenities like a small projector and record player for quiet nights in.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, movie theater, balcony.

Experience penthouse living in this stylish home just three minutes from Shibuya station. The two-bedroom property’s star amenities include the four-person stone bath as well as a spacious tatami room, where you can unwind after a busy day of sightseeing.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, heating.

Taking design cues from Japan’s Kamakura period, this elegant three-story apartment features plaster walls, traditional tatami mats, and a sunken kotatsu dining table. The home’s waterfront location in a more residential area is ideal for peaceful strolls along the river walk path, which is situated just outside the building. (And for stocking up on essentials: There’s a convenience store only a couple minutes away.)

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, waterfront.

For those in search of a break from the city’s fast-paced energy, take note of this calming rental. The home’s decor scheme is defined by its neutral colors and natural textures, from the wood-paneled ceilings to the jute rug and kitchen ceramics. Traditional design details such as paper door panels and light fixtures also help cement a tranquil atmosphere.

Taking the bones of a 60-year-old wooden Japanese house, the Superhost owners of this lovely property kept relaxation top of mind when giving it a modern refresh. Both the dining room and living area are spacious enough for six people to spread out and unwind, and high-quality bedding, toiletries, and furniture ensure a supremely comfortable stay.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, smart lock.

This lovely two-story house was completely renovated in 2024 and offers modern design touches and lots of natural light. House plants are also peppered throughout the space, and the Simmons mattresses are there to ensure guests have the snuggest sleep possible.

Amenities: Washer, high chair, smart lock.

Situated on a peaceful street in trendy Sangenjaya near central Tokyo, this home features plenty of natural sunlight, a handmade wooden staircase and other traditional Japanese carpentry finishes. Modern kitchen appliances and bathroom tiling help to curate a calm environment, while the outdoor patio provides a relaxing space for morning coffee and afternoon drinks.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, dishwasher, outdoor dining area.

Located in the “Little Kyoto of Tokyo,” this brand new home offers easy access to major attractions such as Shinjuku, Shibuya, and Ginza and is within walking distance of the train station. The traditional wooden house can accommodate up to eight guests, and features a luxurious hinoki (cypress) bath as well as an authentic tea ceremony space.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, heating, free parking, private balcony.

With its garden (a rarity in Tokyo) and Japanese artworks guests can actually buy, this home goes above and beyond to provide guests a distinct experience. Request a car service for pickup from Haneda airport for a smoother check-in; when here, you can also request other luxury amenities like a private chef. Whether you’re unwinding in the living room on the curved sofa, or savoring a meal at the long dining table, a stay here is the perfect high-end experience.

Amenities: Washer/dryer, AC, heating, backyard with furniture, smart lock.

In the heart of Tokyo just a two-minute walk from Yoyogi Park, this four-story home is cozy and spacious. All of the bedrooms are aglow in soft light, lending a zen-like atmosphere perfect for falling asleep. Plus, the private balcony comes with outdoor furniture for pre-dinner canapés and cocktails.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, high chair, private patio with furniture.

#6605. Was This the Biggest Week in Sneakers of 2026?

As we inch towards the end of the year, there’s always a massive holiday rush in the sneaker industry (in addition to, well, everywhere else). Annual seasonal drops like the reliable Black Friday and Holiday XI launches from Jordan Brand, plus every major label trying to end the year on the highest note possible, make November and December some of the most exciting times to be a sneakerhead. To be fair, 2026 certainly still has some gas in the tank—plenty of us are already looking ahead to the return of the “Space Jam” Air Jordan 11 next month. Still, this week stands out even in an already crowded release calendar—in fact, I’m inclined to say it’s the biggest and best week of sneaker releases this year has had to offer so far.

Nike and Adidas lead the way with collaborations from massive designers and some up-and-comers alike, including one release that makes a strong argument for being the best sneaker of the year. Reebok’s gradual revitalization takes a massive step in a fun, innovative new direction. And over at Converse, one of the most reliable celebrity designers in the footwear world is dropping some of his best work yet. Start drafting an apology letter to your credit card for everything you’re about to do with it—these are just a few highlights from the biggest, boldest week of sneakers in 2026 yet.

Who said anything about Samba fatigue? Turns out all it takes to make one of the most gen-pop shoes of the last decade feel brand new is a take like the one offered this week by Adidas Consortium collaborator Invincible, a Taiwanese brand that’s quickly establishing itself as a can’t-miss partner for the Three Stripes. Alongside a stellar line of apparel the brand has savvily outmaneuvered any semblance of cultural exhaustion with one of Adidas’s signature silhouettes by keeping it simple: They’ve outfitted the silhouette in a premium black unstructured leather and, bafflingly, a dress shoe sole rather than the Samba’s traditional gum rubber. With perforated Stripes and detailing that mimics those found on dressy leather brogues, it’s an instant contender for sneaker of the year…even if it just barely qualifies as one. This one goes on sale on November13, but with a catch—it’s an Asia exclusive. Pray to the resale market gods.

Nike has been struggling to find their next big-name collaborator, but in the meantime, some old favorites are still holding strong. One of those names is Union, the Los Angeles-based boutique founded by streetwear giant Chris Gibbs. This week, the brand is offering a buzzy iteration on the classic Nike Dunk that comes in a luxe brown suede and a heel-less mule silhouette. Like the Invincible Samba, the MO here is that all it takes to make an old shoe feel new again is a left-of-center take. These are dropping via SNKRS and Union on November 13, for $130 a pop.

Through Reebok’s ups and downs over the last decade, there has been one shining constant: Allen Iverson, the greatest athlete they’ve ever had on their roster. AI’s shoes are always in style, so if the brand simply brought back the original Question Mid silhouette for the shoe’s 30th anniversary, it’d be noteworthy enough. This year, though, they’ve taken the shoe to a new and fairly innovative space, refitting it with modern performance enhancements, making it court-worthy for the first time in decades. Sure, you can still wear them with oversized tees and baggy shorts. But for the first time in ages, the Question could also make it back onto an NBA court (or at least the pavement at your local park). It’s priced at $170 and is available now via Reebok and select retailers.

Ever since he first inked a deal with Converse in 2017, Tyler, the Creator has been one of the best celebrity collaborators in the sneaker biz. This has only become more true since the launch of the 1908 Project last year. The endeavor has seen the pair diving deep into Converse’s archive to revive everything from classic nautical boating shoes, to a jogging silhouette that hadn’t seen the light of day in decades. Ahead of Tyler’s annual Camp Flog Gnaw festival last year, he and Converse launched their best work at the time: the Bronco Boot, a canvas and rubber-toed banger of a sneaker-boot. This year, they’re running it back on a low-top Bronco Boot silhouette—once again ahead of the festival, where we’ll likely see Tyler wearing them. Think of it as the Doc Martens 1461 to the original Bronco Boot’s Doc Martens 1460. Coming your way in four earthy colorways, these are on sale now via Converse.

Speaking of Converse and boots: One of the biggest sneaker stories of the year has been Rick Owens’s return to Adidas after a fruitful stint over at Converse. The designer’s much-anticipated return collection launched this week, with these stunners at the center of the capsule. Debuting on the runway at Paris Fashion Week this past summer, Owens’s Springblade boots are a showstopper of a return. The shoe’s upper is made from a loose textile that fits up over the ankle and a leather toe cap, but the real heat comes in the return of the Springblade sole Owens and Adidas first debuted over ten years ago. They retail for a crazy $850, and can be purchased via the Adidas Confirmed app. Rick’s gonna Rick!

#6603. Elizabeth Debicki Thanks the People Who Opened Doors for Her in Her ELLE Women in Hollywood Speech

Elizabeth Debicki knows that no career is built alone. On Monday night, the actress accepted her honor at ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood celebration, taking a moment to recognize the people who helped make her career possible.

After being introduced by Alexander Skarsgård, Debicki thanked her fellow honorees before reflecting on the support she has received throughout her journey.

“I really love to work. It is my great love,” she said. “And standing here tonight, I feel a really deep sense of gratitude for all the people—the small army of people—who have fought for me to be able to do my work.”

Debicki recalled how casting director Ronna Kress helped her secure an audition for Baz Luhrmann’s The Great Gatsby, which became her breakout film role. At the time, she was just 20 years old, had recently graduated from drama school in Australia, and had never done a screen test.

“Now, Baz, who is my fairy godfather, he fought very, very hard for me after I auditioned for him,” she explained. “But the only reason I was able to get that audition was because Ronna Kress watched the shoddy rookie tape I made back home and somehow managed to convince Baz to sit still long enough to watch it (which, if you know, you know is an actual miracle).”

She continued, “Ronna fought very, very hard for the studio to fly me out here to L.A.—I had never been here before—and to read for the part. And truly, that changed everything. That was really, really my door. And Ronna and Baz, they held that open for me.”

Debicki also praised the other women being recognized that evening: Julianne Moore, Penélope Cruz, Florence Pugh, Inde Navarette, Rosalind Eleazar, and Carrie Coon.

“In your work, your audiences are so privileged to witness your talent and your intelligence,” she said. “And this generosity in the way that you work, it makes us feel sane, and it makes us feel seen. So thank you, so, so much.”
