#6601. The 18 Best Hotels in Tokyo, From Modern Ryokan to Boutique Hideaways

Millions of visitors flock to Tokyo every year to explore the organized chaos that is one of the world’s most populous cities. Whether it’s the tantalizing food scene, trend-bending fashion, or rich history, the Japanese capital entices every type of traveler. Quite frankly, you could spend months here and barely skim the surface. And choosing your hotel can be just as overwhelming as deciding what to cram into a short visit.

Let’s take it one step at a time and start with where to stay. To help you navigate the thousands of options, we’ve narrowed the list down to some of our favorites; they vary in neighborhood, from frenetic hubs to quieter residential enclaves, so the discerning traveler has a lot to pick from. Some are brand new, others are tried-and-true institutions. Many are from familiar international brands, but a few are the dreamy results of home-grown talent.

One thing to note for winter travelers: Keep in mind that New Year is Japan’s most important holiday. While temples and shrines remain open (and are at their busiest), most businesses and cultural sites are closed for several days—even in a city like Tokyo. If you’ll be in town at the start of the year, it’ll be more important than ever to pick the right hotel to keep you entertained.

With that in mind, here’s our guide to the best hotels in Tokyo.

With just 57 keys—making it the second most intimate property within the Four Seasons portfolio after Naviva in Punta Mita, Mexico—the brand’s exemplary service is brought to the next level here. From Sézanne, the hotel’s lauded French restaurant now under the helm of chef Stephen Lancaster, right down to the reception staff who greet guests by name, you’ll be well looked-after.

In theory, a beautifully textured facade made from salvaged tile fragments should catch the attention of wide-eyed wanderers in a neighborhood that is otherwise modern; after all, we’re talking about Ginza. Here, where the goal is typically to shop until you drop, the last thing you’d expect to come across is a ryokan-inspired hotel hidden away on one of the area’s busiest streets. But that’s exactly what gives Fufu Tokyo Ginza that “if you know, you know” badge of honor.

The hospitality brand is known for its intimate onsen retreats in some of the country’s most popular countryside destinations; this is its first urban outpost. There are just 34 rooms, all of which feature furnished balconies dotted with vegetation and hot spring–fed tubs filled with water ushered in from Atami, the birthplace of Fufu Japan. (Either amenity is hard to come by in this city, but both is simply unheard of.) It only gets better when you head to the lush rooftop terrace, where semi-private banquettes hover above a foot bath. Like with any ryokan, half-board options are available and are worth booking. Dinner features either a sushi omakase or a seasonal kaiseki; and as for the breakfast, it’s easily one of the best in Tokyo.

For its inaugural debut in Japan, 1 Hotel set up shop in Tokyo’s Akasaka district, a central hub for business, entertainment, and dining just a stone’s throw away from other popular enclaves like Azabudai Hills and Roppongi. The brand new property opened this past March, with a whopping 211 accommodations that look out to either Tokyo Tower, the Imperial Palace gardens, or the city skyline. In keeping with the brand’s sustainable sensibilities, single-use plastic is non-existent, filtered water taps are installed in every room, and glassware is made from recycled wine bottles. There’s even a farmstand in the lobby featuring fresh fruit that’s deemed “too imperfect” by farmers to sell at local markets—though it looks fairly flawless by this plebeian’s standards—along with more than 1,500 live plants throughout the entire hotel, including the moss that lines the hallways.

Gin fans will delight in the gorgeous lobby bar, where you can choose from nearly 100 locally crafted varieties under a ceiling that’s inspired by karesansui (Zen gardens). At NiNi restaurant, vegetables are the star of the breakfast spread; the rest of the day calls for French Riviera cuisine with a Japanese twist, like a kabocha pumpkin soup de pistou. And if you have time for a dip, you’ll find an indoor pool with a beautiful outdoor terrace just next to the spa.

Every few years there’s a hotel that garners so much attention it becomes an icon before it even opens. In 2024, that title belonged to Janu Tokyo. The flagship of Aman’s long-awaited sister brand, Janu Tokyo trades in zen and serenity for a more energetic approach to hospitality, perhaps best exhibited by the property’s whopping eight food and beverage venues. The hotel also offers a robust wellness center that spans four floors, housing one of the city’s largest gyms, a 25-meter pool, and an extensive spa. Once you’re ready to retire, spacious rooms with largely monochromatic interiors welcome you with soaking tubs and balconies in most instances.

Bookended by action with the heart of Shibuya on one side and Harajuku at the other, there’s a lot happening around Trunk(Hotel) Cat Street. In addition to its stellar location, this lifestyle boutique property has managed to capture the zeitgeist, turning it into a favored haunt for the neighborhood’s effortlessly cool inhabitants. The lobby lounge, with a café by day and bar by night, doubles as a co-working space and is quite the scene at nearly all hours. Upstairs are just 15 accommodations ranging from cozy rooms to residential-style suites, all accented with custom Japan-made adornments utilizing upcycled materials.

The hotel offers two on-site restaurants—one that serves Japanese-inflected international fare, the other a yakitori (skewered meats and vegetables) spot—and its own version of a convenience store with locally sourced bites and a curated selection of sustainable products.

Remote destinations have been a part of Aman’s ethos since its inception—the opening of the Tokyo property in 2014 marked the brand’s first true city project. Resident architect Kerry Hill’s minimalist approach to the group’s luxury-defining properties arguably plays the most natural role in Japan, a country where less is more. The vaulted atrium in the lobby, which is a hot spot for afternoon tea, has become an icon of sorts within Aman’s portfolio, as has the stone-clad, 30-meter pool overlooking the city. Its bright and airy rooms are some of the largest in the city (the smallest coming in at 71 square meters), and are characterized by light wood and low-profile furnishings. Slide the shoji screen back to reveal a stone bathroom, complete with a window-side ofuro tub with uninterrupted views.

Hotel Groove Shinjuku offers a more approachable price point than its sister property Bellustar Tokyo while still benefiting from the same shiny new tower and prime location. Entry-level rooms are cozy, but there are plenty of larger options (at relatively reasonable rates) like the Japanese Suite, which features a tatami-mat floor spacious enough for multiple futons, making it highly popular with families. Colorful carpets accent the otherwise neutral-hued accommodations while the artist-designed suites up the ante on personality. And if you’re here for a lengthier stay, the on-site coin-operated laundry is an unexpectedly wonderful touch.

Top-floor occupancy of a high-rise is commonplace for luxury hotels in Tokyo; it’s no different at the Four Seasons’ second outpost in the city. When you exit the elevators on the 39th floor, you’re greeted by a tranquil water feature that draws inspiration from the Imperial Palace’s moat. In fact, the royal residence (and the sprawling metropolis’ skyline) can be seen from various points throughout the hotel, including the lobby lounge, where afternoon tea is served, and many of its 190 rooms. Speaking of accommodations, they’re spacious here, as to be expected from a Four Seasons, with floor-to-ceiling windows offering plenty of natural lighting and panoramic views. And if you’re looking to set your eyes on Tokyo Skytree, head down to the heated indoor pool for a couple of laps, then cool off in one of the mist chairs.

When hunger strikes there are a few on-site dining options to choose from, including the all-day Italian restaurant Pigneto (the hand-tossed Neapolitan pizzas are the highlight); but the crown jewels are Est and Virtù, both of which are worth visiting even if you’re not a staying guest. At the former you’ll find refined take on contemporary French cuisine with a commitment to sourcing nearly all ingredients from around Japan and a seasonal menu. Meanwhile, the French-Japanese love affair continues at the latter in the form of cocktails, where spirits from both destinations are the star. The Smoked Ume Fashioned is a prefect representation of the concept, which uses a homemade brandy umeshu with plums that have been aged for at least six months, as is the Yuzu Nagi, where yuzu gin meets cognac in a bright, citrus-forward tipple. (Make sure to ask for the seasonal cocktail menu, where you might just find a kakigori-inspired drink, and order the lobster okonomiyaki, an elevated take on the Japanese classic.)

Back in 1962 when Japan was in the midst of an economic boom, the Okura was one of Tokyo’s preeminent hotels, playing host to a number of dignitaries during its tenure. So when it announced its closure in 2015 with a full demolition in tow—on par with the Japanese affinity for rebuilding rather than renovating, as exhibited with the country’s holiest shrine, Ise Jingu—the decision caused quite the stir amongst locals. Nevertheless, the Okura was reborn in 2019 with two glitzy new towers. Some of its history was preserved, like the original mid-century modern chairs that have since been reupholstered, the signature pentagon-faceted lanterns, and kumiko lattice woodwork seen throughout the property.

The main building, dubbed Prestige, is largely geared toward business travelers. The other (the Heritage Wing) appeals more to leisure travelers. All accommodations are suites with sumptuous, oversized bathrooms, complete with a jet tub and private sauna. Some even boast balconies—a rarity in the city. While you’re here make sure to check out Yamazato, a high-end Japanese restaurant with dedicated sushi and tempura counters, along with a visit to the spa for what is arguably one of the better massages in the city.

In a city ruled by skyscrapers, finding some greenery in the middle of Tokyo is like a glass of ice water on a hot summer day. That’s what you get at Takanawa Hanakohro. Part of the larger Prince Hotels compound near Shinagawa Station, the ambiance is set by a classic garden complete with a koi pond, over 200 sakura trees, and the hotel’s very own temple. And while Takanawa Hanakohro occupies one of the complex’s three towers, what makes it particularly special is its 16 ryokan-style suites. Characterized by tatami floors, shoji screens, and large bathrooms with a tub, they’re about as traditional as you get, with courteous service by kimono-clad staff to match. A stay here comes with unfettered access to all of the four executive lounges, including Oh-Sai, which is reserved only for Hanakohro guests, along with a dedicated spa. And while breakfast is usually served at Oh-Sai, you can also request an in-room delivery; the best option, if you’re staying in one of the garden view rooms.

The business district of Otemachi is perhaps one of the most unsuspecting locations for a ryokan, but that’s what makes a tranquil retreat like Hoshinoya Tokyo even more special. Upon entering, the cacophony of the bustling metropolis instantly dissipates and is replaced by a relaxing aura. You’re greeted by a diligent attendant who stores your shoes in one of the bamboo and chestnut cubbies lining the walls, welcoming you to walk barefoot on the tatami mat floors.

With the exception of the restaurants (which includes a recently added sushi bar), the hotel is strictly reserved for guests. And while there are 84 rooms in total, each floor only has six accommodations, creating a sense of intimacy as though every level is its own mini ryokan, along with a shared ochanoma lounge that’s stocked with complimentary snacks like onigiri and an array of seasonal teas. Enjoy spacious digs with low furnishings, deep soaking tubs, and traditional Japanese design elements like shoji screens, but while you’re here make sure to head up to the rooftop onsen and soak in the healing properties of the natural hot spring.

Hoshino Resorts has several brands under its umbrella—including the uber-luxe Hoshinoya—but at the opposite end of the spectrum is OMO, a more budget-conscious collection of hotels that feature compact but well-appointed rooms. At OMO5 Tokyo Gotanda the accommodations start at 200 square feet; ideal for solo travelers who want something more comfortable than a hostel without breaking the bank. Suites are just a little over 600 square feet. Most have sofas by the window so that you can enjoy the city views in comfort, and there is also a bunk-style room that’s great for families or a small group of friends.

But the real highlight here is being immersed in the lesser-explored Gotanda district, where you’ll find culinary gems like tonkatsu institution Tonki, famed reservation-only izakaya Shokudo Todaka, and stand-up udon bar Oniyanma (this particular store is arguably better than its other locations in the city).

Ginza has no shortage of luxury hotels to complement its high-end stores. Just north of the city’s most glamorous shopping district is relative newcomer Bulgari Hotel Tokyo, which opened in 2023. Set directly across from Tokyo Station, the glitzy 98-key property blends its roots with its new environs through contemporary Italian design and time-honored Japanese craftsmanship. Bulgari fans will also appreciate overt nods to the brand in the form of framed sketches from the archives, the jeweler’s 1970s Mount Fuji brooch on display in the gallery, and the house’s signature eight-point star inlaid in the black granite floor of the reception area.

The mark of any stellar city hotel is when it’s enticing enough to keep you indoors despite an exciting metropolis waiting to be explored, and Bulgari Hotel Tokyo delivers. To start, the accommodations are incredibly spacious, starting from 51 square meters. And while there are plenty of luxe touches—throws crafted in Kyoto, hand-brushed gold ceilings, Bulgari-branded bathroom amenities—the automatic blinds are the winner, opening every time you step into the room to reveal panoramic vistas of the city and, in some cases, Mount Fuji on a clear day. Looking for even more dramatic views? Head up to the 45th-floor rooftop lounge, where you’ll be met with Venetian terrazzo flooring and a beautiful glass mosaic wall of birds and trees behind the sleek bar, flanked by lush terraces with plenty of seating looking out to a seemingly endless skyline.

But whatever you do, don’t forget to carve out some time for the spa. There, you’ll find a 25-meter pool clad in reflective green and gold tiles, surrounded by daybeds and floor-to-ceiling windows.

Just blocks from Harajuku and Omotesando Hills, the Aoyama Grand Hotel is arguably one of the most underrated gems in Tokyo. Joining the latest crop of stylish boutique hotels to pop up in the city, the property features plush rooms with mid-century modern decor and punchy patterns that add a quirky character. It offers guests a host of amenities that aren’t even found at hotels commanding double its price tag, such as a complimentary minibar inclusive of alcoholic beverages and snacks as well as bicycles to explore the surrounding area. And while there are a handful of on-site dining concepts, the two standouts are Shikaku, a countertop restaurant serving comforting Japanese fare, and the Top, an alfresco rooftop lounge with a DJ every weekend.

While Shibuya is known for its frenetic energy, things slow down a bit just north of the station in Tomigaya. The trendy neighborhood has been popular for quite some time amongst well-heeled locals, but it’s now drawing in discerning jet-setters thanks to Trunk(Hotel) Yoyogi Park. In stark contrast to its lively and cool sister hotel on the other side of Shibuya, this new property is serene and understated, providing an urban sanctuary just a stone’s throw away from one of Tokyo’s most exciting enclaves. Japandi interiors are the shared work of Keiji Ashizawa Design and Copenhagen-based Norm Architects, setting the stage for a relaxing stay. Its crown jewel, though? The pool club. Open only to guests, the heated infinity oasis looks out at the lush treetops of Yoyogi Park and is complemented by a jacuzzi, sunken fire pit, and oyster bar.

Crowning the new 47-floor Tokyu Kabukicho Tower—where you’ll also find a cinema, nightclub, arcade, and yokocho-style food hall amongst other facilities—Bellustar Tokyo is the perfect hideaway for those who want to be in the thick of Shinjuku without feeling like they are. It’s just steps from the buzzy district’s famed attractions like Golden Gai, a grid of narrow alleys filled to the brim with tiny bars and restaurants, but once you’re whisked up to the sleek lobby, chaos softens into tranquility.

Spacious, minimalist rooms are outfitted with deep tubs and floor-to-ceiling windows to capitalize on their sky-high position (the view alone is worth spending the night in). When it comes to the penthouses, enjoy the benefits of a butler service, a fully equipped kitchen, and access to a dedicated lounge stocked with champagne and small bites. Sora, the largest, also boasts an en-suite spa.

Topping Nihonbashi Mitsui Tower, the Mandarin Oriental is the neighborhood’s premier address. The luxurious group’s signature aesthetic of rich hues and supple fabrics carries over to its Tokyo property with the addition of Japanese design elements like paper lamps and traditional kimono patterns. Spacious accommodations are outfitted with luxurious bathrooms, oversized windows, plush beds, and a bonsai tree for a welcomed touch of greenery. Service, like at any MO, is attentive, and the four-handed massage might be the best way to beat jet lag. While you’re here, explore the immediate area. At the hotel’s doorstep, you’ll find centuries-old businesses still in operation today, a brilliant launching point for discovering Japanese traditions and souvenir shopping.

The Peninsula Hotels has accrued quite a loyal fanbase for its top-notch service, luxurious accommodations with spa-like bathrooms, and its incredible fleet of Rolls-Royces. You can expect all of this at its Tokyo outpost, where doormen donned in the group’s signature white uniform greet you with doors wide open. Rooms nod to Japanese craftsmanship with ajiro ceilings and tochinoki wood doors, and are extremely spacious, with walk-in closets and bathtubs. Beat jet lag with a few laps at the 20-meter pool or make use of your in-room yoga mat and foam roller. Then, head down to the lobby for an unforgettable breakfast. In addition to Japanese and Chinese sets, there’s also a plant-based option inspired by shojin ryori, a Japanese Buddhist cuisine. All three are phenomenal and some of the best in the city.

#6599. The GQ Winter Box Might Not Cure Your SAD, but It'll Come Close

For a limited time, get your first seasonal GQ Box for 60% off ($65 $26) using code GQ60—plus a $25 credit to the Member Store, sent straight to your inbox.

There are two ways to do winter: go out or stay in. We suggest getting good at doing both. The Winter Edit of the GQ Box has everything you need to master the season—from the comfort of your couch or the chill(y) vibes of a night out.

This collection was thoughtfully put together to upgrade your season during a time of year when it seems easier to simply hibernate. Instead, consider this a reason to make the most of it: to take better care of your skin, dress for the weather, get out when the mood strikes, and make staying in something to look forward to.

And while we can’t make the winter any warmer, we can make it a heckuva lot more enjoyable. However you winter, this collection helps you do it better.

Why We Love It: Get serious warmth without sacrificing style. Knit from 100% wool, the Nevis Beanie from Everyday Mountaineering is rugged, comfortable, and versatile enough to work with any fit—and make it look intentionally styled.

How You’ll Use It: Pull it on for cold commutes, morning coffee runs, weekend hikes and any time you need a little extra cold weather protection. And it’s stylish enough to pair with your winter jacket, hoodie, or sweater.

Why We Love It: Minimum bulk, maximum swag. When it comes to the laws of physics—and style—the math on Saddleback Leather’s Newton Wallet checks out. Cut from a single piece of full-grain leather, it’s stitched to last and keep everything streamlined. Genius.

How You’ll Use It: Keep essentials in the card slots, tuck cash into the center pocket, and because full-grain leather only gets better with age, expect to carry this one long after your holiday shopping’s done.

Why We Love It: Your drink, your rules. Whether you’re hosting or settling in for a cozy night on the couch, Rabbit’s Houdini Noir set, with its sleek matte black finish, brings bartender-worthy gadgetry to every cocktail or zero-proof mocktail you mix.

How You’ll Use It: Measure your pour with the jigger, shake things up with the cocktail shaker, and strain into your favorite glass for a bar-worthy finish. This compact tool set is everything you need to make every sip better.

Why We Love It: The unsung hero of a good fit is a great pair of socks. Goldtoe has perfected the standard—thanks to 90 years in the game. Breathable cotton, cushioned sole, built-in arch support, moisture-wicking tech, and that iconic reinforced gold toe make for the perfect sock.

How You’ll Use It: This short crew height works with practically everything from sneakers to boots, making them perfect to layer whether you’re going for an outdoor hike or just hiking over to the office. Pull ’em on and step out with confidence wherever your day—or feet—take you.

Why We Love It: You get ready for the day and then life happens. A sweaty workout, a packed commute…and suddenly, you could use a refresh. This body and hair mist is just that, with bright citrus, warm hinoki notes and skin-care-like ingredients that hydrate from head to toe.

How You’ll Use It: Keep it in reach for those moments when you need to freshen up but don’t need a full shower and outfit change. Spray through your hair and body, and you’re set.

Why We Love It: Winter skin has different needs, and your GQ Box delivers either way. Whether you want to focus on body hydration with Mitchell & Peach’s English Leaf Body Souffle or facial hydration with First Aid Beauty’s Ultra Repair Face Moisturizer, these picks help keep dryness in check during the colder months.

How You’ll Use It: Smooth the body souffle over your skin after a shower, or work the face moisturizer into your daily skin-care routine. Whichever you chose, you’ve got your winter hydration covered.

Why We Love It: Call it mistletoe insurance. Davids Hydroxi Toothpaste helps freshen breath, fight plaque, whiten teeth and support enamel health—all without preservatives and totally ready for you to get up close and personal.

How You’ll Use It: The natural spearmint helps keep your breath fresh and your smile ready for close conversations—whether that’s before a holiday happy hour, end-of-year chats with your boss, or an evening spent mixing and mingling.

Why We Love It: If winter has a signature scent, this might be it. Commodity Spice Expressive layers saffron, cardamom, nutmeg and cinnamon sugar over warm tonka bean and sandalwood for a scent that’s spicy, smooth, and feels tailor-made for dropping temperatures.

How You’ll Use It: Just a spritz or two adds the perfect amount of warmth. Unwrap your scarf, take off a layer, and the fragrance projection gets you noticed without overpowering the room.

Why We Love It: No one likes an uninvited guest—especially of the acne variety. Luckily, Hero Cosmetics Mighty Patches get to work in as little as six hours, absorbing the gunk and helping shrink the look of pimples. Consider the zit officially evicted.

How You’ll Use It: Spot a pimple popping up before a big meeting, date or party? Stick one of the patches on clean, dry skin and then leave it alone. Peel it off in the morning—no picking or poking required.

Why We Love It: Winter weather can take a toll on your skin, so consider this your seasonal upgrade. Omic+ Skincare’s 10% Tranexamic Acid Face Serum helps brighten, while DIME Beauty Co.’s Luminosity™ Eye Serum targets puffiness and dark circles. Two smart additions to your winter skin-care lineup.

How You’ll Use It: We recommend working these into your routine as soon as—or even before—the effects of winter weather start showing up. Apply the face serum before your daily moisturizer or dab the eye cream under eyes and let the formulas work their magic.

#6596. 10 Airbnbs in New Mexico to Book This Winter, from Santa Fe and Beyond

There’s something undeniably magical about New Mexico, especially in the colder months. Chile ristras line front porches, ski season revs up in Taos, and farolitos light the streets in December. The days are sunny and dry, but nights are cold enough for a kiva fireplace or a hot tub soak under the stars. It makes for a different kind of trip than a cozy New England getaway or fall foliage-inspired cabin retreat, the desert awash in sunset hues. Plus, New Mexico is prime road-trip territory, with its wide-open highways and dramatic landscape shifts.

From the powdery white dunes of White Sands National Park to the art-saturated streets of Santa Fe, the state has inspired artists and creative types for years upon years. Whether you want to lose yourself in the vast vistas that captivated Georgia O'Keeffe or spend a long weekend gallery-hopping and market-browsing in Santa Fe, we've rounded up a selection of Airbnbs that feel as distinctive as the state itself to serve as your home base.

Ahead, 10 New Mexico rentals that sit at the intersection of design and desert living.

Artfully designed by fashion designer Raquel Allegra, the 8,000-square-foot space sits on five acres in a quiet canyon about 20 minutes from Taos Ski Valley. The interiors are anchored by signature New Mexican architectural features such as arched windows, white plaster walls, high ceilings, and wood-burning kiva fireplaces, while the furnishings are design-forward yet restrained, allowing the home’s bones to really sing.

With six bedrooms, it’s an expansive enough space for a ski trip with friends or a creative group retreat; one Vogue writer even booked it for an off-the-beaten-path bachelorette. Radiant heated floors and a steady supply of firewood keep the home toasty after a day on the slopes. And with no cell service available near the home, it’s very much your chance to completely unplug.

Amenities: Radiant heating, wood-burning kiva fireplaces, furnished porch, WiFi, garden views

Location: Taos Ski Valley, Taos, New Mexico

This 1940s Santa Fe adobe, once a corner store, is now an art gallery-like home whose walls are dotted with more than 50 nichos (small, recessed niches carved into the plaster). They’re a staple of Southwestern and Spanish colonial architecture, each lit like a museum case and, in the case of this property, filled with ceramics and other artful pieces.

Polished white cement floors and a white oak kitchen give the entire home the feeling of a clean palette; a calming backdrop for whatever your Santa Fe vacation holds. Its four bedrooms make it a good fit for a family ski trip, with Ski Santa Fe 30 minutes away and a hot tub and fire pit waiting in the private backyard for your return. The River Trail is a block away, Canyon Road is close by, and dogs are welcome.

Amenities: Kiva fireplace, hot tub, firepit, soaking tub, chef’s kitchen, gated parking, dog-friendly

This hacienda was once a neighborhood shop where horses and burros carrying firewood were hitched out front. Today, sunny windows open onto a bright living room, and the house has three kiva fireplaces, shelves packed tightly with books and board games, and a renovated kitchen you can make your own during your stay.

Between the three bedrooms and the den (which has a sofa bed), this home sleeps eight, and two adjacent units can be rented for larger groups. Galleries and restaurants are right on its doorstep, too.

Amenities: Three kiva fireplaces, Sonos sound system, renovated kitchen, two private patios, washer and dryer

This listing has been high up on our Airbnb wishlist for years. Located in Abiquiu, not too far from O’Keeffe’s famed Ghost Ranch, this adobe sits squarely in the middle of 10 shared acres in the high desert landscape that drew O'Keeffe (and generations of artists and photographers after her) in.

This recently renovated home is a quiet base for exploring one of New Mexico's most creatively charged regions. The traditional architecture is intact with thick walls, desert light, wood beams, stone fireplaces, and classic New Mexican tile floors. The interiors are peppered with both man-made and natural relics, like a Noguchi-style hanging paper lantern or a sculptural tumbleweed hanging from the ceiling. It’s the kind of place O'Keeffe herself might have booked.

Amenities: Full kitchen, washer/dryer, mini-split AC and heating throughout, mountain views, dedicated workspace, WiFi

Designed by architect Bart Prince and featured in Architectural Digest, this sculptural home at the base of the Sandia Mountains is definitely a one-of-a-kind experience. Six viewing decks offer panoramic views of the mountains above and Albuquerque's city lights below, while floor-to-ceiling windows blur the line between indoors and out. A private hiking trail on the property connects directly to Sandia Peak; meaning the National Forest is essentially your backyard.

Amenities: 6 viewing decks, private hiking trail, floor-to-ceiling windows

Location: Sandia Mountains, Albuquerque, New Mexico

This mid-century adobe sits in Casa Alegre, a leafy pocket of Santa Fe’s Midtown District, where you’re a block from the River Trail and close to the galleries and shows at the El Rey. A traditional kiva fireplace anchors the living room, Sonos speakers run throughout, and one of the bedrooms comes with a cozy reading nook. With three bedrooms and a fully fenced yard, it works well for families young kids who want their own space for their holiday in the desert. On winter nights, the hot tub will be an especially beloved feature.

Amenities: Kiva fireplace, hot tub, Sonos sound system, fenced yard, washer and dryer, parking for three cars, dog friendly

Casa de la Cruz is a traditional adobe, built with stucco, giant vigas, and thick walls that stay warm in winter and cool in summer. The interiors reflect the Southwest aesthetic with wrought-iron light fixtures paired with Navajo blankets and pillows, leather sofas, and rustic, worn furniture sprinkled throughout.

Set on 12 acres abutting Carson National Forest in Abiquiu, the property has three kiva fireplaces, radiant heated floors, and a private box canyon to explore—which is an incredible selling point on its own. Plus, you can’t beat the location with Ghost Ranch being just 30 minutes away, the hot springs of Ojo Caliente another 30, and downtown Santa Fe under an hour, as well.

Amenities: Private box canyon, outdoor fire pit, full kitchen, outdoor grill, Starlink WiFi, 3 fireplaces, radiant heated floors

This charming home is located in Dixon—a small artist's village in the hills of Northern New Mexico—with wilderness walks straight from the door. The bones are traditional New Mexico adobe architecture with viga ceilings, Southwestern decor, works from local artists, and a newly remodeled kitchen. Surrounded by pinyon and sage bush views alongside the mountains, its exceptionally quiet and gorgeous sunsets are best taken in from the plush ramada with its built-in banco seating.

Amenities: Ramada, full kitchen, streaming TV, AppleTV, WiFi, central heating, pet-friendly

Featured in Dwell, this off-grid Earthship (a fitting description) outside Taos is a rare rental that beautifully intersects luxury and sustainability. The structure collects rainwater, generates its own solar power, grows food indoors, and uses water three times over—all without sacrificing comfort. Adobe interiors, a south-facing greenhouse, and whimsical touches (like a stained-glass mermaid) keep things interesting in the best way.

Amenities: Off-grid solar power, rainwater collection, indoor greenhouse, turntable, bluetooth, WiFi

This newly built guesthouse is part of the H.H. Dorman estate, rumored to have hosted D.H. Lawrence, Georgia O'Keeffe, Ansel Adams, and Aldous Huxley in the 1920s. The two-bedroom, two-bath home, which shares the grounds with the historic main house, is a short walk to Santa Fe plaza and features vaulted ceilings, a gas fireplace, one-of-a-kind antiques, and art throughout. It boasts two private courtyards, one with an outdoor dining area and another with a fire pit and hot tub, which guests are welcome to enjoy.

Amenities: Private hot tub, fire pit, two courtyards, full kitchen, gas fireplace, washer/dryer, gated parking

#6595. Patrick Schwarzenegger Says This Small Detail Makes All The Difference In A Great Martini (Exclusive)

Three years with one of vodka's oldest families will apparently teach you a few things.

Patrick Schwarzenegger knows a thing or two about a good martini. After three years working with Ketel One and spending time with the family behind the vodka, the White Lotus actor has learned that some people take their cocktails very seriously.

"I'm not that severe," Schwarzenegger told me, although he's developed a few preferences of his own. His biggest? "A frosted glass. A cold glass I think makes all the difference."

I caught up with Schwarzenegger in Schiedam, Netherlands, during a Ketel One-hosted visit to the historic Nolet Distillery, where the family has been making spirits since 1691. The trip was actually his idea. After hearing so much about the distillery from the Nolet family, Schwarzenegger wanted to see everything firsthand, even getting his hands dirty by shoveling coal into the distilling equipment.

According to Schwarzenegger, family members have gotten so particular about their drinks that they'll check where a bar stores its vermouth, olives, and white wine before ordering. If certain ingredients have been sitting out rather than refrigerated, they might opt for a drier martini.

Bob Nolet sees that same attention to detail in the way people order cocktails today. "Today's martini drinkers know what they want," he told Delish, whether that's a classic dry martini, something dirty, or an espresso version.

Of course, that hasn't stopped bartenders from seeing just how far they can stretch the definition of a martini. Schwarzenegger told me he tried The Corner Store’s viral sour cream-and-onion version largely because he'd heard so much about it, something he deemed “really good.”

The Tomatini was another story. He appreciated how convincingly it captured tomato flavor, but the novelty only went so far. "I think that I could have that for a few sips, maybe one max, but then I'm tapped out of that," he said.

His more dependable order is an espresso martini, something the Nolets know particularly well. Schwarzenegger revealed that the family even arranged for espresso machines to be sent to his wedding in Idaho, giving guests a way to enjoy his favorite cocktail during the celebration.

For Carl Nolet Jr., the connection goes deeper than a shared appreciation for espresso martinis. "Patrick comes from a family that is equally committed to their craft in the entertainment space," he told Delish. "You can see that commitment through his career and how he brings his legacy into a new generation."

Carl also credits Schwarzenegger with offering a younger perspective on cocktail culture, particularly how drinking has become part of the way people socialize, host, and celebrate.

For someone who knows his way around a cocktail, Schwarzenegger doesn't actually drink all that often. Between filming, fitness, and work, he's made a rule to keep alcohol to weekends. He's also taken an interest in the growing demand for better-for-you options, pointing to canned cocktails with less sugar and real fruit juice as examples of how people's drinking habits are changing.

That curiosity extends well beyond the bar. With his involvement in the protein snack company MOSH, Schwarzenegger has become the kind of person who considers wandering supermarket aisles a perfectly good Friday night activity. One of his first stops after arriving in the Netherlands was a grocery store, and he loves comparing what's available in different places, from Los Angeles to wife Abby Champion's home state of Alabama.

His Instagram algorithm isn't helping matters, either. Food, drinks, random syrups—if an ad catches his attention, there's a decent chance it'll end up on his doorstep. "I buy everything," he admitted.

Interestingly, all that enthusiasm for trying new things doesn't necessarily translate to elaborate dinners. He and Champion love exploring restaurants together, but they're equally happy cooking at home or keeping things simple. She's a fan of Chick-fil-A and In-N-Out, while he's perfectly content with a plate of chicken and rice.

After talking martinis with Schwarzenegger and the Nolets, I might start paying a little more attention to what happens behind the bar. I'll leave the vermouth inspections to the professionals, but keeping the rest of my martini on ice until I'm ready for a fresh, frosty glass? That's a level of service I could get used to.

#6594. The Greatest Grand Theft Auto Missions, Definitively Ranked

Grand Theft Auto VI drops on November 19th, and there are many ways to prepare. I’ve been replaying every game going back to the original, with a particular soft spot for the 3D era: III, Vice City, and Rockstar's greatest achievement, San Andreas—yes, yes, I'm coming in hot. After some 13 years of GTA Online, with its perpetual content stream and microtransactions, it’s easy to forget how it all began. The franchise has consistently brought freewheeling chaos and mayhem, sure. But it has also always delivered memorable story missions, which evolved from basic lures and assassinations into something like GTA V's “Friend Request or “Reuniting the Family,” culturally scathing mini-movies which have to be played to be believed. “My least favorite mission involves Michael using a tattoo gun on me,” former Rockstar director, writer, and producer Lazlow Jones told me of the latter mission. “I still give Dan [Houser] shit about that one to this day.”

What follows is a ranking of the greatest missions in the series’ history, with one caveat: I only allowed myself four missions per game, maximum. To help sort through the clear classics and happy accidents, I talked to some of the people who made these games come alive, including Jones, former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, and West Coast rapper Young Maylay, the beloved voice of Carl Johnson. Shockingly, Maylay says he’s still fond of the infamous “Wrong Side of the Tracks.” “All we had to do was follow the damn train, CJ!” Maylay said, imitating his exasperated sensei Big Smoke. I’m not including that mission on here, though, partly because I’d like to make it out of this piece alive.

Bum. Budupup-budum. For a lot of us, that theme was the beginning of our Grand Theft Auto journey. What follows is barely prologue. There's an ambush on the Callahan Bridge, an escape with 8-Ball, and a drive to a safe house in Portland, Liberty City's Brooklyn-by-way-of-Queens industrial borough. You do not fire a single shot. And yet each playthrough already looked different. Did you open the short manual and splay the map across your bedroom floor, or drive blind to the edge of the Red Light District?

"The most memorable mission for me was the first one I ever played, 'Give Me Liberty,'" Lazlow told GQ. Once the host of Technofile, a syndicated show about technology and video games, Lazlow showed up at Rockstar’s Manhattan offices in 2001 to report a radio piece. Not long after, he was spoofing American radio himself as the iconic voice of Chatterbox FM.

"[Rockstar co-founder] Terry Donovan brought over a copy of the game the day it came out. Dan [Houser] had given me a PlayStation 2,” Lazlow continued. “I'd worked on the radio for the game all summer with Dan but I hadn't actually seen it. After the cinematic ended, I got into the car and Head Radio came on and I'm driving through town. It blew my mind."

Crazy what a difference three years can make. The Donald Love of GTA III is a composed real-estate scion with a media empire. Liberty City Stories, set in 1998, shows you the man before the polish, who’s way more overt about his hunger for power — and human flesh.

The mayoral race is his project, and Toni Cipriani is his instrument. Toni guns down the incumbent mayor R.C. Hole, somehow engendering only one star. "Steering the Vote" then puts him behind the wheel of a campaign van, zooming across Staunton while the loudspeaker blares: “O'Donovan is a communist!” “O’Donovan hates America!” or “A vote for Love is a vote for happiness!” The van has to reach specific stops before the messaging triggers, which means the game is literally grading you on how much of the world you can seduce. GTA may have predicted everything from Ozempic culture to billionaire doomsday prep, but there was no forecast sharper than this one.

For most of Rockstar’s history, the studio—technically a U.S. company, but with a British development team—has made its bread and butter satirizing America, and nothing has been off the table. But in London 1969, the first of two expansion packs for the original Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar transplants its crime sandbox to London in the late ‘60s, where the Brits take center stage. (“Who gave Paul McCartney a shotgun?” one YouTube commenter asks.) Broken up into chapters, the seminal “Dead Certainty” draws on the high-flying exploits of the real-life Kray twins, the foremost perpetrators of organized crime in London’s East End at the time, who rubbed elbows with politicians and entertainers before ultimately being locked away for life.

Grand Theft Auto is a game about many things, but one of the first things it was—and still is—is a game about cars. If San Fierro’s underrated main story missions aren’t enough (yes, I know, Cesar. The yay is leaving San Fierro again), head on over to Easter Basin for the best edition of “Exports and Imports.” The concept dates back to the original GTA, where it was called “Crane Bonuses,” but it’s a classic here because of its sheer scale. What starts at the docks turns into a mad hunt across the entire map of San Andreas, finding and then delivering 30 specific vehicles.

San Andreas has 212 defined vehicles, more than twice as many as Vice City. You start learning the taxonomy—how to tell a Remington from a Sabre and an Infernus from a Cheetah—and figuring out where certain vehicles turn up. The Camper can be found on top of Mount Chiliad, meaning the hard part isn’t finding it so much as getting the lumbering thing back down in one piece. When I was younger, I never really appreciated these side missions. Now, I love how they slow the game down and make you observe all the GTA sandbox goodness you might otherwise race past.

Rockstar has a long, cruel history of giving you a remote control and trolling. But unlike “Supply Lines” or “Demolition Man,” there’s a certain genius to this one. Vic Vance pulls up outside the Mendez compound and, instead of going in like a cowboy, climbs into a van to command a newfangled robot servant, Domestobot. At this point the game becomes a butlering simulator: Fetch a drink, light a cigar, and clean the floor, all the while trying to crack a drug kingpin’s basement safe. Rockstar didn’t forget about our charming robot after this, either. In GTA V, Radio Los Santos host Big Boy laments the Domestobot future that never arrived: "We have internet glasses, but not our own robot butler!”

In 1995, at age 17, Blair Renaud joined what became Rockstar Canada (now Rockstar Toronto), and stuck around long past his original contract, eventually becoming a technical director. “I basically walked into the boss's office and was like, ‘I'm not leaving. I'll do whatever you want,'” Renaud told me. After designing the London ‘69 map without ever having set foot in England (“I just winged it”), he and his entire Toronto office were put on QA duty for Grand Theft Auto 2, with its grim retro-futurist Anywhere City and sharper graphics.

GTA has always played with consumption (Donald Love likely ate his real estate mentor, Avery Carrington) but “Hot Dog Homicide!” is GTA2 at its most dastardly. In the original PC/Dreamcast version, you steal a bus, load it with civilian passengers, and deliver them to a Russian mob boss's meat grinder to satiate his army. “I think [GTA] was actually more controversial [in the beginning] about the crime, rather than just the violence,” Renaud said. “It was like ‘Oh, I'm like stealing people's cars and running them over.' It was a little bit more real.” For all the creative choices the series has been pilloried for in the ensuing years, a mission like “Hot Dog Homicide!” wasn't nearly as explosive then as it would be today.

I always get excited about missions that let you revisit a location you've already seen, especially when the game gives you a reason to see it differently. “Bury the Hatchet” sends Michael and Trevor back to North Yankton, the snowy Midwestern state where GTA V began, where the two men start digging into the events of the botched bank heist that set their lives on their current course.

It’s San Andreas’s “St. Mark’s Bistro” done better. Instead of briefly dropping you into a familiar location for a quick hit of nostalgia, GTA V actually lets you spend some time knee-deep in the snow. Michael and Trevor each retrace the events of the heist; Trevor unearths a coffin marked with Michael’s name, only to find Brad’s decomposing body inside. Ultimately, the two men aim guns at each other. Michael has spent much of the game on his high horse insisting that he’s changed, while Trevor, always the firecracker, is at least honest about exactly who he is.

Another great LCS mission that adds to Liberty City lore. Donald Love sends Toni to explosives expert 8-Ball (who still has functioning hands at this point) to raze an entire neighborhood, Fort Staunton, and pave the way for his Panlantic deal. With the Forellis giving chase, Toni has to get a van loaded with explosives to the site, then race through tunnels planting charges beneath the neighborhood. No way those tunnels aren’t at least a little inspired by Die Hard with a Vengeance. After the biggest explosion in GTA history (not bad for a PSP game), the National Guard can be found roaming the neighborhood. And by GTA III, Fort Staunton is teeming with scaffolding, construction pits and Cartel members, a neighborhood still reshaping itself after Toni’s seismic contribution.

There are few things more San Andreas than being handed a shoddy military plane by a mysterious government agent and being told to fly it across the state without being detected by radar. “N.O.E.” is the greatest test of your skills acquired in the Pilotwings-esque gauntlet, “Learning to Fly.” Fly too high and the military shoots you down; fly too low and the terrain dings you first. The mission captures just how far Mike Toreno has pulled CJ from the streets and into the shadowy world of government conspiracies.

Greg Johnson, a hip-hop journalist who became Rockstar's senior researcher from 2003 to 2020, traces those wild Toreno missions to the 1992 film Deep Cover. Most people know it through its title song, Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg's first record together. But the film itself touched on government corruption and drug trafficking in Southern California.

“Loved that Dan [Houser] put some Deep Cover-inspired missions in GTA SA with Mike Toreno basically playing Agent Carver and CJ as John Hull,” Johnson said. “I definitely talked to [Houser] a lot about Deep Cover, but he was also having conversations with [West Coast hip-hop producer and Rockstar writer] DJ Pooh, who personally knows [drug lord] Freeway Rick [Ross] about that era, and reading up on books and reports…as they wrote the game.”

Heavy metal band Love Fist is in a pickle. Think Speed, only with a limo, and even thicker Scottish accents than Groundskeeper Willie. The mission is straightforward, but not easy: drive the limousine across the city while keeping the momentum steady enough to hold off detonation. It’s also a testament to how Vice City could turn even its tertiary characters into stars. Love Fist barely occupies a sliver of the game, yet they've stuck around as memorable rockstars for more than two decades. Obbe Vermeij, longtime Rockstar North technical director, also has a soft spot for the mission. “Particularly funny,” he notes, “because the Love Fist voices are just guys from the office.”

There isn't a single on-rails shooting sequence in Grand Theft Auto that I've ever passed easily. Doesn't matter how many times I've played. I’m no deadeye. Luckily, in “Reuniting the Families,” there’s plenty packed in before we get to that. This is back when CJ, Sweet, Ryder and Big Smoke are all still homies, and when the vast map of San Andreas is still centered on the few-mile radius around Grove Street. You head to a motel with the intention of saving the hood, only to find it crawling with SWAT. After battling your way through the rooms and taking down a helicopter on the roof, you escape by car with the cops still in pursuit. Smoke is behind the wheel while an AK with unlimited ammo is placed in your hands. The cops can even climb onto the car and try to wrestle the gun away from you. It’s a wild, arcade-style sequence, but also one of the last hurrahs for the homies before betrayal and more nonsense from that bastard Frank Tenpenny. Fittingly, the getaway car flies straight through a Sprunk soda billboard reading “A Taste of Things to Come.”

“Cop Land” is peak bromance between Tommy and Lance, before the latter decides to ruin the movie. It’s also a snapshot of just how much more active and assertive Vice City’s main character is than man-of-no-words Claude, made all the more credible by the late Ray Liotta’s swagger in the role. Tommy isn't merely taking orders and working his way up someone else's criminal ladder. By this point, he's building the Vercetti Estate into his own empire and making his own destiny.

In “Cop Land,” the entire northern portion of the first island experiences a demographic shake up and now consists of exactly two assets: cops on foot in tan and brown and cops in green police cruisers. First, Tommy and Lance have to steal cop uniforms, a step that can get clunkier than it should when the garage door won't shut with the right number of cops inside. From there, you head to North Point Mall in disguise, plant a bomb and hightail it out of there with a five-star wanted level. Vice City’s officers were particularly bloodthirsty, and getting to a Pay 'n' Spray with Lance still intact—my man is drawn to dumb deaths—was one of my greatest teenage achievements.

Dubai-born real estate heir Yusuf Amir can buy anything. So naturally, the thing he wants most is an experimental attack helicopter parked on an arms dealer’s yacht. Rockstar was mining Gulf excess for laughs more than a decade before Dubai Bling and Love Is Blind: Habibi. Yusuf’s gaudy apartment tells you everything you need to know about him. There’s a miniature model of Algonquin laid out in his penthouse, as if the entire city were already one of his properties, and a giant dollar sign mounted on the wall. He dances to “Arab Money,” peppers his speech with hip-hop slang, and adopts the mannerisms of a culture he knows nothing about. Luis, unsurprisingly, is not particularly moved.

That makes “Sexy Time” the perfect introduction to him. Boat out from the marina, slip past the patrol and steal the Buzzard. Only, mid-flight, Yusuf calls and asks you to turn around, blow the yacht apart and run down what’s left of the arms dealers. For those who felt GTA IV took itself way too seriously, The Ballad of Gay Tony was a breath of fresh air. “Yusuf Amir is one of my all time favorite characters Dan [Houser] created,” Lazlow said. “The dialogue in this mission is hysterical, and he's constantly trying to sound street while going on about building luxury condos.”

The final chapter in the InterGlobal Studios asset arc turns Vice City into a formidable platformer. Tune in to Flash FM (Talk Talk’s “Life’s What You Make It”) or Fever 105 (Kool & The Gang’s “Summer Madness”) as Tommy leaps across rooftops on his trusted PCJ-600 bike in a single bound—though it’s far more likely that you’ll tumble to the streets at least once. There’s a delicate balance required for each stunt jump, but also a sense of reward once you master timing and speed.

This mission is, as the kids say, vibes. Something about scaling the ‘80s skyline by night while the rest of the city sleeps is unforgettable, along with the hilarious payoff, when Tommy triggers a spotlight that projects a massive X-rated image promoting adult performer Candy Suxxx (née Candice Shand) onto the side of a building. The most memorable GTA characters have a way of appearing in multiple forms: voices on the radio, bodies in cutscenes and, here, as advertising beamed across the world itself.

Small-town America gets the GTA treatment in “The Paleto Score.” Michael, Franklin and Trevor roll into sleepy Paleto Bay to rob the Blaine County Savings Bank, but the getaway quickly becomes less Ocean’s Eleven and more like Terminator or even MechCommander. Even before the heist, Lester, the master of elaborate setups, proves to be an unlikely master of conflict resolution too. His dry little “Hello, Franklin” to break up another Michael and Trevor spat still has me in stitches.

What starts as a relatively conventional bank job becomes a slow, lumbering march through an entire town, with our antiheroes mowing down cops, SWAT and eventually the military along the way. There’s even a reward for going overboard. One of the gold-medal requirements is to fire more than 4,000 bullets — because apparently, just robbing a bank wasn’t impressive enough.

Every time we see our hippie friend The Truth, his missions get better. In the apex of his mission tree, “Black Project,” CJ infiltrates Area 69, Rockstar’s twist on Area 51. There’s a stealth way of entering the maximum security facility, but that’s not nearly as fun as going in guns blazing. The level abounds with hilarious one-liners (“Get the General Mills on the line!”) and lab announcements (“Tonight’s menu is posted in the canteen. Barf bags can be ordered from Human Resources.”).

After GTA III’s and Vice City’s limited interiors, San Andreas gives you lively environments like Area 69, where you can disappear down corridors, into laboratories and through underground tunnels. And once CJ steals the coveted jet pack prototype, it becomes a way to fast travel across the state of San Andreas, bringing a whole new perspective to the final hours of the game. “The Truth. He stayed high as a motherfucker talking about conspiracy theory shit,” Young Maylay said. “But he would hit it on the head.”

Niko spends much of GTA IV doing other people’s dirty work. By “Late Checkout,” the diamond deal has gone so badly that Ray Boccino has lost his money, his diamonds and what remained of his patience. Isaac Roth, the diamond dealer who helped blow up the deal, is hiding in the Majestic Hotel. Ray wants him dead.

This mission is a choose-your-own-adventure affair. You can take the elevator and fight your way up through the guards, floor by floor, or use the window-cleaning platform outside to reach the penthouse from above and then fight your way back down. Either way, Niko eventually has to work his way through the hotel, killing Roth and his associates before making his escape.

It’s Rockstar’s take on the Plaza Hotel, minus Tim Curry, turned into a bonafide shooting gallery. Bonus points if you shove the front desk manager, who may respond by hopping over the desk to fight his own bellman.

Phil? Phil Collins? That's right. The former Genesis drummer and self-styled “Little Elvis” made gaming history by becoming the first real-life celebrity to lend his name and likeness as well as his voice to GTA. Like Vice City, VCS is inspired by the ‘80s TV drama Miami Vice; Philip Michael Thomas, who played Ricardo Tubbs on the show, voices Lance Vance in both VC and VCS, and Collins, as it happens, guest-starred on the series in 1985, as con man Phil Mayhew.

In this mission the Mob is after the Brit, and Vic has to ward them off. It all comes to a head during “In the Air Tonight” at Hyman Memorial Stadium. You're up top clearing Forelli saboteurs looming in the rafters while Phil is down below working the crowd.

For the man voicing Vic, this history wasn't lost on anyone. "Miami Vice was literally my favorite show as a little boy," said voice actor Dorian Missick. "I still have pictures of me in what I call my Miami Vice suit. One year, my mom let me get a little suit that they used to wear, but the collar’s turned up. I wore something like that for Easter. So to me, it was my opportunity to kind of be on the Miami Vice episode that I never got a chance to do. So all of these things, the Phil Collins of it all, and just that energy of it — it was exciting to be a part of that."

“Caida Libre,” Spanish for “free fall,” is one of those missions that finally makes the sprawling expanse of GTA V’s San Andreas feel like one cohesive playground. Michael and Trevor are hired by Martin Madrazo to take down a plane carrying his cousin Javier. Michael starts things off by shooting at the aircraft from Galileo Observatory with a sniper rifle.

The best part is the handoff, a seminal showcase of GTAV’s character-switch mechanic. First, Michael is coolly shooting down a plane from a mountaintop, and moments later you’re controlling Trevor, flying down country roads on a Sanchez motorcycle, chasing the falling debris like a man following his destiny. Eventually, Trevor finds Javier, kills him and climbs into the wrecked plane to retrieve the package. And, because this is Trevor, the mission ends with Trevor pining after Martin’s wife, Patricia, and kidnapping her. So much for the moral of Obsession.

When GTAIII first dropped, I spent the first few hours of the game gazing longingly across the river to Staunton Island, imagining what came next. Back in those days, Grand Theft Auto’s world opened up in stages and phases, trusting players to forgo instant gratification. That little stretch of water felt like the portal to another world entirely.

After Claude is victim of a double-cross, Maria helps him flee from Portland to Staunton where he meets his next boss, Asuka. But here’s the rub: Claude first has to prove he’s no longer the Mafia’s strongman, which means gunning down the beloved don Salvatore Leone in the heart of his turf. Once the deed is done, the Leones turn on you for the rest of the game, transforming the St. Marks neighborhood into a veritable “shotgun hell,” as YouTuber The Professional dubbed it in a video rant a few years ago. “Sayonara Salvatore” is thrilling enough. But its lasting impact on the open world is what players still can’t stop talking about.

If “Three Leaf Clover” feels familiar, that’s because it is. The mission is Rockstar’s loving homage to Michael Mann’s Heat. Niko joins Packie McReary and his brothers to rob the Bank of Liberty, complete with suits, masks, enormous bags of cash, and a getaway that quickly turns into a war through the streets of Liberty City.

There’s a little Point Break in there too: A civilian tries to play hero inside the bank, killing Michael Keane before being killed himself, echoing a similar moment in the 1991 film. Then comes the seemingly endless firefight through Algonquin’s neighborhoods, followed by an escape into the subway tunnels — the best transit system, by the way, in GTA history.

Vermeij says that in GTAIV, missions were often centered more around story than gameplay, but both are top-notch here. “These scripts could get quite big,” he said. “Thousands of lines in some cases…With every fix the script got a little more complicated.” This is GTA IV at its most cinematic, channeling the American crime movies and cop thrillers that have long shaped the series, all the while paving the way for GTAV’s slew of heists. “Four Leaf Clover,” though, remains the gold standard.

#6593. Pamela Anderson Is a Sentimentalist at Heart

The actress on holiday traditions, motherhood, and the sentimental value of giving with Pandora.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

For Pamela Anderson, the holiday season is less about elaborate celebrations and more about appreciating life’s quieter moments. “I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul,” she tells ELLE. Whether she’s tending to her garden on Vancouver Island, cooking vegetarian dishes for her family, or watching her sons establish traditions of their own, Anderson has found a new appreciation for the simple pleasures that make this time of year so special.

It’s a philosophy that extends to her approach to gift-giving. A self-described sentimentalist, Anderson prefers presents that carry a personal meaning, from family photographs to jewelry passed down through generations. And through her partnership with Pandora (Anderson is a face of the brand), she’s found a way to celebrate those connections with pieces that feel both personal and accessible.

I love the fall. I always say fall is the season of the soul. I think that’s a Virginia Woolf quote. Even in a garden, you focus more on the little things instead of being overwhelmed by so much abundance. It feels like a really special time of year. I love the fall weather and the leaves changing. It’s beautiful, especially here on the East Coast. Where I’m from on Vancouver Island, it actually looks very similar.

I absolutely love gardening. When I was home, I was cleaning up a bunch of leaves, and it feels like a workout, too. It’s nice to be outside, even in the rain. I don’t shy away from the rain, or nothing would ever get done where I’m from. I love being outside and getting my hands dirty. In this part of my life, I’m really gravitating toward that, but I’m also working a lot, so it’s a really good balance. I get to do really glamorous things, work on film and onstage, and then I go home, put my boots on, and get in the garden.

Now, the boys are usually with their wife and fiancée over the holidays. They’re building their lives and their own traditions, so I always say, “Don’t worry about me. I’m always around.” It’s nice to see them building those traditions. I’ve done a lot of hosting and party planning in my life. I’m a decorator, so I love all of that. But this year, it’s really about seeing all the traditions and things my sons have soaked up and watching them start their own lives. I’m not a pressure planner. I don’t want them to feel pressure to include me. I just say, “You guys do your thing. I’m watching, I’m observing.” It’s really special as a mom to see them so happy with their significant others. The women in their lives have great taste and love to share that with them and me.

I love cooking. I always cook all the sides, the vegetable dishes. It’s been a while since we’ve all been together for a big meal. Time is just flying by. My sons are such great cooks, too. We all have our specialties. I think I actually prefer decorating to cooking, because you set the stage. Then you can have a potluck!

I’ve given a lot of my jewelry from my lifetime to my kids and to their wife and fiancée. I like more sentimental gifts. I’m a sentimentalist, I guess. I love flowers, and this year, one of my sons just got married, but they don’t have wedding pictures of themselves. So they’re getting wedding pictures, engagement pictures, just a bunch of really sentimental things from me.

I just give my kids everything. I like to give those pieces to them so they can appreciate them while I’m here. I don’t hoard a lot of things. I’m always changing, always trying new things, and I don’t think I’m a big consumer anyway. I have special pieces that I’ve already passed on.

My mother always wants my Pandora jewelry. Every time I go anywhere, she’s asking, “Do you have Pandora? Do you have any earrings?” She loves it. My mom’s sisters and everyone just love Pandora. She loves both gold and silver, the jewels, the colors. Some of the beautiful pieces they have around the holidays, she would go crazy for. She loves it all.

I definitely wear more jewelry than I used to. It depends on what I’m wearing or where I’m going. I like to recycle jewelry. A lot of my Pandora pieces I’ve worn on different red carpets or to different special events. It’s nice for jewelry to be attainable, cruelty-free, and sustainable. Those things are so important to me. Jewelry isn’t just for the few. It’s for everybody.

When I align with somebody, I like to know that we have similar philosophies. I think it’s the small-town girl in me who never felt jewelry was in the cards for her. It’s nice to know there’s a jewelry company that’s forward-thinking and sustainable, thinking about recycling and also making it affordable. It just feels more like me. I love glamour and I love fancy things, but I think my kind of fashion is more inspirational.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
