#6592. Where to Stay in Jamaica for a Tropical Winter Sun Getaway

If you’re anything like me, entering the land of 4:50 p.m. sunsets means it’s time to a) cry a little and b) book a tropical vacation as soon as possible. In my experience, Jamaica has always been the perfect antidote to cold-weather blues; I’ve been nearly every winter for the past decade. This season, the island is still rebuilding after Hurricane Melissa made landfall last October, but its recovery—and tourism comeback—has been inspiring. Jamaica truly has it all, from iconic music and fashion to pristine beaches, lush rainforests, fresh (and absolutely delicious) food, and a long tradition of Hollywood and royal cachet.

As for where to stay? The boutique hotel scene is unmatched. While Jamaica does have its fair share of big-box, could-be-anywhere all-inclusives, the top hotels are the complete opposite and ooze charm.

Whether you want to drink rum punches on the cliffs of Negril, go hiking in the lush jungles of Port Antonio, or simply hang on the beach as the soft sounds of reggae drift through the air, these 12 options make it easy to experience the country’s vibrant creative culture for yourself. Just be prepared to get hooked, if you aren’t already.

Unless you live your life like a disgruntled White Lotus guest, it’s basically impossible to be in a bad mood at Rockhouse. Located on the western tip of Negril, the 40-room hotel—which celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2024—has all the ingredients for a good time. It’s built into Negril’s limestone cliffs, for starters, so the cliff jumping is next-level. The stone and thatched-roof villas are thoroughly charming; many of them have bright red ladders that allow you to climb directly down into the turquoise sea (which you should, especially first thing in the morning after a steaming mug of Blue Mountain coffee…heaven). The food is great, too, with fresh local dishes like callaloo omelets and moringa smoothies made with ingredients from the property’s on-site organic garden.

But really, you book this spot for the energy. Artists, designers, and other creatives frequent the property for its lively atmosphere and stylish crowd. I’ve personally stayed at Rockhouse twice myself—first with my mom and sister for a mother-daughter trip, and then with my two best friends for our 40th birthdays last year—and it was all smiles both times. My girlfriends and I still reminisce about our endless rum punches at the infinity pool bar, where the bartenders were so much fun, we momentarily forgot our bodies cannot handle mainlining cocktails like we once could. Luckily, that’s what hangover swims are for.

Amenities: three on-site restaurants, spa, infinity pool, weekly psilocybin sound bath experience, complimentary shuttles to Skylark Negril, daily morning yoga, candle-making workshops, and Rockhouse Foundation community tours

Bonus tip: The traditional bathing soak at the spa is heavenly: Tubs are filled with flower petals, herbs, botanicals, and your choice of aromatherapy oil.

Address: West End Road, Negril, Westmoreland

While the cliffs at Rockhouse are undoubtedly delightful, sometimes you just want to spend the day on the sand. And for that, Skylark—which opened as Rockhouse’s sister property in 2018—is the perfect choice. The 43-room boutique hotel holds a prime location right on Seven Mile Beach; not just a beach, but the beach in Negril. Skylark’s spot in the sand stands out for its yellow-and-white striped umbrellas and aqua loungers that match the sea.

Venture past the beach and you’ll notice the hotel’s mod, tropical design. While Rockhouse leans more rustic, Skylark is a bit of a throwback, with a very retro Miami Beach feel (think: black-and-white checkered floors and pops of pastel pink). And then there’s the Miss Lily’s of it all. Back in 2011, the team behind Rockhouse opened the Jamaican restaurant in Soho to bring the spirit of Rockhouse back home to New York, where it quickly acquired a cult following. So when Skylark announced it would open the first Miss Lily’s outpost in Jamaica itself, the superfans went wild—myself included. I’ve been twice now, and must say it feels extra special to enjoy their signature jerk chicken with a side of tropical breeze. Once the sun goes down, DJs take over with nightly sets of the country’s latest reggae and dancehall.

Amenities: rooftop spa, complimentary beach loungers, tents, and umbrellas, boutique and gift shop, beachside service from Miss Lily’s, daily shuttle to sister hotel Rockhouse

Bonus tip: Don’t miss the boutique’s Sweet Like JAM section, featuring high-end designers from across the African and Caribbean diaspora (like Diotima, Tribe Nine Studios, Theophilio, and Bianca Saunders), all curated by stylist and fashion editor Mecca James-Williams.

Address: Norman Manley Boulevard, Negril, Westmoreland

The secret’s certainly out about Geejam. This secluded hilltop hideaway is located in Port Antonio, a port town on Jamaica’s lush, lesser-visited northeastern coast. Built by two former music executives as a residential recording studio in 1998, the property eventually expanded into a boutique hotel in 2008 and has hosted everyone from Bad Bunny to Rihanna to Amy Winehouse (to Drake, Megan Thee Stallion, Harry Styles, Florence and the Machine, The Rolling Stones…the list goes on).

But despite its celeb appeal, Geejam somehow retains has the feel of an undiscovered gem. There are four wooden jungle cabins (named Ska, Rocksteady, Mento, and Drum & Bass, after Jamaica’s popular music genres), 12 guestrooms, a three-bedroom villa, and two premium villas with a dedicated staff. Many are built into the property’s six acres of rainforest so discreetly, you could miss them if you’re not looking. The main open-air bar and lounge, Bushbar, is just as low-profile: When my husband and I dropped in for a cocktail on a recent visit to “Portie,” (as the locals call it) we wondered if we were in the right place. A few guests were playing pool on the vintage billiard table, others were milling about the actual pool deck, and mellow reggae was playing softly in the background. Surely, we thought, a hotel this legendary would feel a bit more…scene-y? But of course, that understated vibe is precisely the point. It extends to the property’s new restaurant and bar, Bentley’s, which opened on their private, tucked-away beach in 2025 and serves a mix of Jamaican specialties and homemade pizza.

Amenities: recording studio, private beach with kayaking and paddleboarding, outdoor infinity pool, two main restaurants/bars, spa services, gym with private trainers available to book, pool table, treehouse DJ booth, various wedding and event spaces

Bonus tip: Portland is known for its waterfalls, rainforest hikes, river rafting, and iconic spring-fed Blue Lagoon—so tempting as it may be to hole up in your cabin, be sure to explore a little, too (the hotel’s custom excursions team can help with that). Don’t miss fresh lobster from Cynthia’s on Winnifred Beach; just call her a day ahead to place your order.

Address: 122 Skippers Boulevard, Port Antonio, Portland

Most people who visit Jamaica tend to stick to the main coastal towns of Negril, Montego Bay, Ocho Rios, and Port Antonio. But the country’s lush Blue Mountains—home to the legendary, eponymous coffee—are worth adding to your itinerary, too. And there is no better introduction to their misty magic than Strawberry Hill.

Set on a former coffee plantation just 10 miles above Kingston, the hilltop retreat is the go-to hotel in the Blue Mountains. A trip here begins with a steep, 45-minute drive up from the city (the hairpin turns and winding rainforest roads are part of the fun), but it really kicks off once you take in the sweeping panoramas from the top. The 26-acre property is centered around a sleek infinity pool that overlooks Kingston and the Caribbean Sea. The pool area feels especially glamorous at night, thanks to the city’s twinkling lights in the distance and the sound of clinking silverware from the on-site restaurant (get the rum cake for dessert). All 12 Georgian-style cottages and villas also have verandas that overlook the mountains and gardens. And for the birders among us, Strawberry Hill is home to 24 endemic species of our favorite friends, including the Doctor Bird, the country’s national bird.

But the biggest allure may just be the music history. Island Records founder Chris Blackwell purchased Strawberry Hill in 1974, and his influence is felt throughout the hotel, from the gold and platinum records on the walls to the vintage black-and-white photos of Bob Marley and other artists (Marley actually recovered at Strawberry Hill after he was shot in 1976, and his time there famously inspired him to write “Natural Mystic” later on). My husband and I loved sitting at the bar with a Blackwell Rum Punch, naturally, and chatting with the bartender about all the other musicians who’ve stayed there through the years: Peter Tosh, Yoko Ono, Mick Jagger, and many more.

Amenities: infinity pool, mountainside spa, yoga pavilion, on-site restaurant, landscaped gardens, bar with a fireplace and vintage piano, hiking trails

Bonus tip: Order a pot of Blue Mountain coffee to your room each morning, and enjoy it on your veranda while soaking in the strong morning sun. There’s something about drinking Blue Mountain coffee straight from the source that just hits different.

Address: New Castle Road, Irish Town, St. Andrew

For those immersed in the Jamaican hotel scene, GoldenEye needs no introduction. The legendary property on Jamaica’s north coast is filled with lore, starting with its origin as James Bond author Ian Fleming’s private retreat, which he built in 1946. Today, the property is owned by none other than Island Records founder Chris Blackwell, who bought it in 1976 and later made it part of his Island Outpost portfolio (along with Strawberry Hill and The Caves in Negril).

Glitzy history aside, it would be hard to have a bad time at GoldenEye. The property is practically set up to lower your cortisol, with 45 accommodations spread across 52 acres that include lush tropical gardens, quiet beaches, and its star attraction: a protected lagoon. Whether you opt for a lagoon cottage with a private dock, a beach villa right on the sand, or Fleming’s villa itself (a splurge, to be sure), there is truly no bad option here. Guests can even kayak across the lagoon to their spa appointments.

Amenities: swimmable lagoon, two freshwater swimming pools, saltwater splash pool, spa, boutique, private beaches, tennis court, pickleball court, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, snorkeling equipment, Sunfish and Hobie Cat sailboats, two on-site restaurants, one on-site bar

Bonus tip: Be sure to spend time at Bizot Bar, GoldenEye’s casual beach restaurant named after the late counter-cultural journalist Jean-François Bizot (who was good friends with Blackwell). The breezy soundtrack comes courtesy of Radio Nova, a Paris-based radio station founded by Bizot that plays an eclectic mix of world music.

Address: Race Course, Oracabessa, St. Mary

Owned and operated by the Morrow family for nearly 70 years, Jamaica Inn is filled with family traditions, like a succession of pet black labradors all named Shadow (the first Shadow dates back to the 1970s). The beach bar, Teddy’s, is named after longtime bartender Teddy Tucker, who joined in 1958. Many of the staffers have worked there for more than 30 years, and notable guests include Marilyn Monroe, Katharine Hepburn, and Winston Churchill.

All history aside, the hotel is also just a beautiful spot that lends itself to a properly lazy time. Located in Ocho Rios, a resort town on Jamaica’s north coast, it’s spread along a private beach often considered to be one of the best in the Caribbean, with 700 feet of soft golden sand and pristine turquoise waters. On top of that, all 55 suites, cottages, and beachfront bungalows have direct views of those waters—and many have private plunge pools as well. They even have a no-screen rule, meaning there aren’t any TVs, radios, or clocks in the rooms to remind you of life outside your seaside bubble (whether or not you choose to surrender your phone to that rule is up to you). If you can manage to pry yourself away from the “beach-eat-repeat” lifestyle, Jamaica Inn has an array of activities to explore, from James Bond film showings on the sand to a tour of the hotel’s cannabis farm partner, Jacana, which includes a lesson on the history of Rasta culture.

Amenities: outdoor pool, spa, croquet lawn, garden tours, daily afternoon tea presentation, yoga pavilion, library, boutique, fitness center, complimentary daily activities, nightly live music

Bonus tip: Music lovers must take a field trip to nearby Nine Mile, the birthplace of Bob Marley.

DJ and music producer Diplo once told Vogue that his personal style is “kind of random; it does whatever.” But judging from his private (yet rentable) retreat, Pompey, his design style is far more considered. Set on 62 acres of private land in lush Port Antonio, the eight-suite property—which opened in 2024—is more like a Brutalist creative compound than a hotel, one where everything is intentionally set up to help you channel Jamaica’s artistic spirit. There’s a recording studio, naturally, complete with professional gear, and an impressive list of extras, from ping pong and chess to a wet bar with stocked snacks and an outdoor wooden deck overlooking the rainforest. There’s also an outdoor yoga pavilion, an equestrian center, and a two-floor gym with wellness facilities including hydrotherapy, infrared sauna, and skincare treatments with products from the legendary Dr. Barbara Sturm. All stays come fully staffed with daily housekeeping and a full-time chef, who, instead of supplying menus, cooks based on the vibe of the day.

Designed by Brooklyn studio Freecell Architecture and architect Gia Wolff, the concrete retreat is meant to both blend into nature and look striking against it. Centered around a saltwater infinity pool, the property stretches out into a regenerative farm and orchard with all sorts of walking paths, ATV trails, and direct access to Port Antonio’s beautiful San San Beach. Even if you’re not blessed with a productive burst of creativity while you’re there, you’ll likely still leave feeling relaxed and at peace—a win, either way.

Amenities: recording studio, on-property helicopter access, saltwater infinity pool, yoga pavilion, gym, equestrian center, ATV access, E-bikes, walking paths, regenerative farm and orchard, concierge-led programming

Bonus tip: To book, email Pompey’s concierge directly through their website. Rooming configurations are quite flexible, so tell them exactly what you’re looking for and they will set you up accordingly—they can even arrange additional accommodations five minutes away for larger groups.

Address: Fairy Hill, Port Antonio, Portland

Mention Treasure Beach to anyone familiar with Jamaica, and they will likely think of Jakes. Since its opening in 1993, the 60-room boutique hotel has become something of a treasure in Treasure Beach—pun very much intended—and it’s not hard to see why. Founded by Jamaica-born artist and designer Sally Henzell, Jakes reflects her creative sensibility everywhere you look. The bungalows, cottages, villages and rooms are painted in a rainbow of colors, and they’re all decorated with local art. Like most of Jamaica’s south coast, Jakes was hit hard by Hurricane Melissa last year, but fortunately, it began welcoming guests again that December and fully reopened in March with reimagined oceanfront bungalows. Its whimsical design is still a big part of the appeal.

The other main appeal? Treasure Beach itself. Unlike some of Jamaica’s more tourism-oriented hubs like Montego Bay and Ocho Rios, Treasure Beach is quite low-key. There are a few guesthouses and restaurants, but mostly it’s just rocky coastline, houses that dot the fields, and splashes of magenta bougainvillea. No all-inclusives, no cruise ships. For book lovers, the property hosts the Calabash International Literary Festival every other May. It’s drawn a glittery crowd over the years, from authors (Zadie Smith, Marlon James, and Padma Lakshmi, to name a few) to guests including Angelina Jolie.

Amenities: private beach and dock, freshwater pool, three restaurants, ocean-facing spa, seaside yoga deck with daily sessions, gift shop, monthly full moon dinners, on-site art classes

Bonus tip: Take the complimentary boat trip to Floyd’s Pelican Bar, Treasure Beach’s iconic thatched-roof bar that sits on stilts in the middle of the sea. It was fully destroyed by Hurricane Melissa, but has since reopened.

Address: Calabash Bay, Treasure Beach, Saint Elizabeth

While Montego Bay has its fair share of standard all-inclusives, Round Hill is anything but. Set on 110 lush acres of former pineapple groves, the storied boutique has been the go-to spot for an elegant stay in the area since it opened in 1953. John F. Kennedy and Jackie Kennedy honeymooned there, and Meghan Markle and Prince Harry have visited, too. But no guest is more associated with the property than Ralph Lauren. He visited for the first time at Christmas in 1978 and loved it so much, he proceeded to buy two cottages there: High Rock in 1982, and White Orchid in 1996. In the early 2000s, Lauren even redesigned all 36 rooms in the main hotel (known as the Pineapple House), as well as the cocktail lounge, which is considered to be the original Polo Bar. His touch is evident in the country club style that runs throughout: white stone floors, four-poster mahogany bamboo beds, and the green-and-white striped awnings.

Aside from those 36 Pineapple House rooms Lauren designed, there are also 27 individually-owned villas, ranging from two to six bedrooms. Travelers also book Round Hill for its impeccable landscaping and fresh feel. It’s an extremely well-manicured resort, after all—one where lush gardens seem to stretch on for miles and open skies are never hard to find. Add an array of activities to the mix—including tennis, pickleball, and river rafting—plus island fare from the property’s 11 dining options, and you’ve got everything you need for an idyllic tropical stay.

Amenities: spa, fitness center and fitness classes, outdoor infinity pool, walking trail, water sports facility, house reef, boutique, chef’s garden, events pavilion, daily complimentary afternoon tea, nightly entertainment

Bonus tip: During the festive season, Round Hill hosts daily cocktail classes at 3 p.m., where you can learn about the history of Jamaican rum and Blue Mountain coffee—and make your own cocktails, of course.

Address: John Pringle Drive, Montego Bay, Hanover

Set on 400 acres along two miles of Montego Bay coastline, Half Moon has been a resort mainstay on Jamaica’s north shore since it opened in 1954. It’s known for its whitewashed cottages, wide verandas, and unmistakably grand feel. JFK stayed there (the man clearly loved Jamaica!), as did many members of the British royal family, including Queen Elizabeth II, then-Prince Charles, and Prince Harry. Sadly, because Half Moon is quite open to the elements, it was hit especially hard by Hurricane Melissa last year, which caused extensive damage to the property and personally affected more than 850 of its team members. Some villas reopened in April after a major restoration effort, but the historic resort just announced that most of the remaining property will reopen by Thanksgiving, followed by the final batch of cottages by the festive season. That includes a mix of rebuilds, redesigns, and new additions like Garlandstone Gallery, which will sell local art.

Half Moon is particularly strong in the tropical activity department: golf, tennis, pickleball, water sports, locally inspired spa treatments, and excursions that go deeper into Jamaican culture are all available. I especially loved the farm-to-table vegan dining experience at Stush in the Bush, an organic farm and restaurant in the lush fields of St. Ann. Think crispy plantain chips, wood-fired pizza, and skillet cornbread, all served with herbs from the garden and their own line of gourmet sauces and spreads.

Amenities: private beach, infinity pool, swimming coves and lagoon, spa, golf course, equestrian center, tennis and pickleball courts, water sports, sailing and diving classes, sea turtle releases, on-site garden, fitness studio, 10 bars and restaurants, children’s village

Bonus tip: The hotel’s collection of paintings from Montego Bay artist Michael Lester is now available for purchase. Lester, who died in 1972, is known for his expressionist paintings of Montego Bay and Jamaican life.

Address: Rose Hall, Montego Bay, St. James

Plus, the cabin itself is incredibly peaceful. With a lush garden filled with birds, plants scattered throughout the home, and exposed cedar beams in most rooms, it feels like a true city oasis. Perhaps best of all? The cabin is located directly under a mango tree, so you get a real taste of island living. (The owner, Terryon, may even greet you with a fresh mango smoothie.)

Amenities: Outdoor shower, HDTV, AC, backyard, outdoor dining furniture, hammock, free parking

If you’re looking for the perfect spot for a tropical group getaway, say for a birthday or a bachelorette, look no further than this massive Airbnb in Negril. Set beneath a grove of palm trees just steps from the famed Seven Mile Beach, it sleeps up to ten people and comes fully staffed with a private chef, butler, and housekeeper. There’s a gorgeous pool with loungers, and a large outdoor dining table perfect for long group dinners.

All five bedrooms come equipped with a four-poster king bed, private bathroom, private terrace, and ocean views—here, there is no surrendering to the “bad room” just to make someone else happy. There are also multiple hangout rooms for lounging, all with an airy, white-on-wood tropical design and colorful artwork on the walls. Reviewers are especially into the butler service, with one saying her butler would just “appear at the beach” with a carafe of hot coffee anytime hers was running low (Jamaican hospitality at its finest). And to really take any possible friction out of your group stay, you can even arrange for the kitchen to come pre-stocked at an additional cost.

Amenities: Chef and cleaning available during stay, pool, AC, washer, TV, bar, outdoor furniture, beachfront access, kayak, free parking

#6590. Don't Miss Starbucks Red Cup Day 2026—Here's What You Need To Know

It’s the most wonderful (and caffeinated) time of the year.

Starbucks has already unveiled its 2026 holiday cup designs, including an adorable miniature version for dogs. Now it's time for the humans to get their hands on something they can actually keep.

Starbucks Red Cup Day is officially back, and the multinational coffeehouse chain is once again giving customers a little something extra with their seasonal caffeine fix. But before you make a special trip for a little piece of festive plastic, a few things are worth knowing, as your usual coffee order might need some adjusting.

Circle Tuesday, November 17, on your calendar, as that's when Starbucks will be handing out its latest reusable holiday cups at participating locations across the country.

The catch is that it’s only happening while supplies last. And considering how much people love free stuff, I wouldn't recommend waiting until a 4 p.m. coffee run to try your hand at getting a cup.

Starbucks says it's bringing in extra baristas for the occasion, too, which should help with the inevitable rush of customers looking to add to their collections.

You'll need to purchase a qualifying handcrafted holiday or fall beverage of any size. Yes, even a tall gets you the same free 16-ounce cup as someone ordering a venti.

You don't even have to physically step inside a Starbucks, either. Orders placed at the drive-thru, through the app, or via DoorDash, Grubhub, and Uber Eats are all eligible.

And somehow, brewed Starbucks Christmas Blend and Starbucks Reserve Christmas coffee don't qualify, despite having Christmas right there in their names. Because apparently, even Christmas itself can't get you a free cup.

This year's version features coffee cherries and leafy branches tied together with a big red bow. There's also a green-and-white ribbon design around the outside that ties into the rest of Starbucks' holiday collection.

The reusable cup is made with 95 percent recycled material, and unlike the paper versions you normally toss after finishing your latte, this one is meant to stick around.

In fact, putting it back to work comes with a few perks. Bring a clean reusable cup to Starbucks on a future visit, and you'll save 10 cents on your drink, while Rewards members also get double Stars on their entire order.

#6588. Teyana Taylor Kicks Off the Holidays in True Maximalist Fashion

She attended the Burberry holiday party in fringe-trimmed fur

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The temperatures are dropping, string lights are hanging from the trees, and Christmas music is taking over shopping malls, which means the holidays are just around the corner—and Teyana Taylor is getting in the spirit early. Showing up to the Mark Hotel in New York City, the actor celebrated the forthcoming season with Burberry, wearing a cozy statement coat from the house’s Fall/Winter 2026 collection.

The piece in question—the Linley wrap coat—put a winter twist on the classic Burberry trench. Crafted from brown shearling, it featured a long-length silhouette that mirrored that of its rainwear precursor, reinterpreting the signature style just in time for the label’s 170th anniversary this year. Where khaki-colored epaulettes and belted cuffs might typically sit, the outerwear featured deep-brown leather alternatives. And while the traditional trench’s edges would be hemmed, here, they were trimmed with fringe. The number was finished with a silk lining.

Underneath, Taylor wore leather pants, which she tucked into matching knee-high leather boots with a sculptural flared heel. She added rounded sunglasses, while pulling her curly hair into an updo. As for her glam, she went full-holiday mode with sparkly lipstick and zig-zag nails. She posed in front of an oversize Christmas tree covered in red ornaments, from tartan bows to berries.

At the Burberry event, the star—who recently celebrated her graduation from Auguste Escoffier School of Culinary Arts—was joined by sibling duo Apple and Moses Martin, The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney, Claudia Sulewski, Rob Lowe, and more friends of the house.

#6587. Vogue France Head of Editorial Content Claire Thomson-Jonville’s Guide to Megève

To be sure, there’s no shortage of quaint, storybook villages in any part of the Alps—but over on the French side, tucked away in the Haute-Savoie region, there’s something special about Megève. “I’ve been coming for years; I enjoy it just as much in summer as in winter,” says Vogue France’s Head of Editorial Content, Claire Thomson-Jonville. “I love that it still feels like a small, cozy village. It’s postcard-perfect with a family-friendly atmosphere; it’s discreet, not flashy, with incredible nature.”

While the hiking—and generally stunning landscape—is a great draw for year-round tourism, travelers in the winter really have one reason to visit: the skiing. Thomson-Jonville has her routine down: “One of my favorite things to do is to take a moniteur de ski for the day and head into the mountains, around Mont d’Arbois.” (On her more adventurous days, she’ll brave the challenging pistes a little farther out at Mont Blanc.) In between stints on the slopes, she’s developed a list of local favorites, for everything from designer fashion to where you can find the best raclette; ahead, she offers us a peek into her Megève address book.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Allard is a classic—a Megève institution. It’s on the square beside the church, the maison behind the original ski fuseau created in the 1930s. It’s a lovely place to find a beautiful sweater. Blu&Berry is where I go to find something more unexpected; they have pieces from The Row and Celine. Big Boss is another Megève institution, with a great skiwear selection. It’s one of those shops that everyone who comes here regularly knows.

For a worthwhile investment piece: The Hermès store in Megève is particularly well-stocked, and the Loro Piana boutique in the center of the village is great for après-ski shopping!

For unique souvenirs: Again, Allard for something classic that feels connected to the village. For something more unusual, there’s Max et Isa; it’s great for antique jewelry, vintage Murano lamps, and decorative objects. It’s a good address to browse for an unusual gift or a special piece for your chalet.

For the magpie: Guilhem Joaillier is my favorite jewelry store in Megève. I’ve picked some meaningful pieces here over the years; it’s a solid gift shop, too. Someone always has a birthday when we’re in Megève, and, of course, there’s always Christmas.

For your next great read: Scarlett Megève has a good curation of art books, as well as fun decorative objects. It’s a good place to buy gifts. The Maison de La Presse in town is the place we all go to buy magazines and novels; it’s super simple but you’ll always bump into someone you know there. Megève is a small place!

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: I spend a lot of time in the Pharmacie de la Tour on Place de l’Église—it’s full of little treasures. I love an après-ski French pharmacy haul. Vitamins, moisturizers, supplements, hair masks… I love trying out new products when I’m in the mountains.

For a pick-me-up treat: Le Hibou Blanc is a great address for brunch or a coffee. It’s in the center of town with a big, heated terrasse to sit outside with a cappuccino and watch the world go by.

For a luxurious lunch: L’Idéal 1850, up on Mont d’Arbois, for a lunch break between runs with a beautiful mountain view. It’s very social; wear a great ski outfit the day you book a table.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Le Vieux Megève. It’s a cheerful, traditional spot in the village—it’s noisy, yummy, and so much fun. Book early to share a raclette or fondue with family or friends. It’s my favorite spot in Megève—in fact, everyone in my family loves it there. It’s a unanimous favorite.

For a different kind of evening, I love Kaito at the Four Seasons. The sushi is delicious, and it’s a bit of a scene. Dress up and people watch!

For a post-slope spa day: I always love to try new places, but to me, Les Fermes de Marie has the best spa in Megève. The facials are great. The Susanne Kaufmann spa at Les Chalets du Mont d’Arbois is also good for bodywork.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: The bar at the Fer à Cheval. It’s cozy and welcoming—a perfect place to settle by the fire after a day in the mountains, plus it’s in the center of town. The bar at the Four Seasons after dinner is also a vibe for the people watching.

For your packing list: My mountain packing list is tried and tested: One ski look, one puffy ski jacket, a (fake) fur coat, cashmere joggers, and big sunglasses. I also pack UGGs and cashmere socks for warmth, plus some great earrings to liven up a low-key dinner look.

#6586. How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”

But embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

It’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

And so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we launched, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very quickly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We launched overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some issues we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process showed with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

Then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

That’s very well said. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really showed through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

We saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

We only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

It’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on issues “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Routine Excellence with Real Live Astronaut Reid Wiseman.”

#6585. Upside-Down Apple Cider Cheesecake

If you feel there’s never enough graham cracker crust with your cheesecake, then this version is for you. The entire no-bake cheesecake is surrounded by crust, so there are buttery graham crackers and creamy cheesecake in every single bite. The exterior isn’t just hiding a silky-smooth cheesecake filling, but also a surprise syrupy apple filling. If you want to win the holidays this year, set this unassuming dessert on the table and watch everyone ooh and ahh as they cut in and discover the sweet, spiced, and completely delicious treat hiding inside.

How to make it upside-down:To achieve a double layer of crust, you need to freeze one layer so that it’s easy to place on top of the cheesecake. Before serving, you’ll flip the whole thing onto a plate, which puts the seam on the bottom and gives you a beautiful display of a solid crust. It’s easier than you think to flip it, and the parchment will ensure nothing sticks to the springform pan.

Make ahead & storage:I love to make this dessert during the holidays because you can prep and make it all ahead of time. The apple filling can be made up to 3 days ahead, and the assembled cheesecake can be made up to 2 days ahead of when you want to serve.

#6583. Bernadette’s Charlotte and Bernadette de Geyter’s Guide to Antwerp

“Antwerp is a small city with so many big stories,” says Charlotte de Geyter, co-owner of Bernadette, the Antwerp-based fashion label she founded with her mother, Bernadette. The best way to see it all? Slowly; and if you’re anything like the mother-daughter duo, by bike.

A hub of creativity, the Belgian city has real fashion bonafides; it counts Ann Demeulemeester and Dries Van Noten among its graduates, the best-known of whom are the subject of the current “Antwerp Six” exhibition running at the MoMu Fashion Museum through January 2027. There’s never been a better time to visit; come winter, the city slows down and gets even cozier. “One thing that embodies the Antwerp spirit to me is its quiet confidence,” continues Charlotte. “The city has always been home to incredible fashion designers and artists, and I think that creativity still defines Antwerp today.” Below, read Charlotte and Bernadette’s recommendations for where to eat, shop, and souvenir hunt in Antwerp—plus, what to pack for a trip to town.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Expect a strong focus on high fashion and directional pieces at Renaissance, a boutique known for championing emerging designers and young brands, all curated with a distinct point of view. And no trip to Antwerp is complete without visiting the iconic Dries Van Noten store. Decorated by Gert Voorjans, the interiors feel both theatrical and deeply personal, true to the spirit of the brand.

For vintage gems: Rosier 41 is a long-standing vintage designer store where you’ll discover an exceptional selection of second-hand Belgian fashion. Antwerp has a deeply rooted fashion culture, and the store reflects that, full of unique archival pieces and rare finds.

For a worthwhile investment piece: The destination in Antwerp for established luxury designers and international fashion houses is Louis. I would invest in Belgian designers like Margiela.

For the magpie: Go straight to the diamond district in Antwerp, near the station.

For your next great read: Eric Tonen Books in Kloosterstraat for art books, and the bookstore inside the fashion museum MoMu for the best fashion books.

For stylish home goods: We love the smaller boutiques like St Vincents, as well as antique shopping in Kloosterstraat.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Take them to buy Christmas ornaments in Christel Dauwe for a truly unique experience.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: Le John is a go-to for a low-key dinner. Quiet, simple, and consistently good food; the kind of place you keep returning to. Order the pumpkin tortellini, a delicate handmade pasta filled with sweet pumpkin served with rich sage butter, with a good glass of red wine.

Decorated by Axel Vervoordt, Sir Anthony Van Dijck is an Antwerp institution that has a timeless atmosphere and remains one of the city’s classic dining rooms. Go for the seasonal menu, featuring refined Belgian-French dishes made with fresh ingredients (and a great tarte tatin).

For a bakery treat: The “Een Strik” from Dellafaille is a go-to—it’s a bow-shaped pastry made from delicate, flaky puff pastry, with a golden, caramelized exterior and a light, buttery crunch.

For the art-lover: My partner, Ben Sledsens, works with the Tim Van Laere gallery. They truly put the artists first and host new exhibitions almost every month. We also love Cour Space, a young, more conceptual gallery showcasing emerging artists and contemporary practices. The space feels intimate and understated, with carefully curated exhibitions that attract Antwerp’s creative crowd.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: Tango Bar is a favorite. It’s a newer, trendier restaurant by two young entrepreneurs, with interior design by Cami Verborgh. Expect a more fashion-forward crowd here.

For your packing list: There’s a deep sense of history; you feel it most while slowly wandering through the old streets on a quiet weekend, surrounded by beautiful, historic buildings. In the winter, this means you’ll need a good raincoat, and boots for lots of walking (A.F. Vandevorst is a classic Belgian option). Don’t forget a comfortable pair of jeans and a warm cashmere sweater.

#6581. Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond

After a whirlwind month of speculation, unsubstantiated rumors, and endless Kalshi prognostication, white smoke has finally emerged from the Amazon MGM chimney. There’s a new James Bond—and his name is Robert Pattinson.

The announcement ends the long-running—and quite frankly, exhausting—mystery over Daniel Craig’s successor and starts a new creative era for the 007 franchise, which Amazon acquired from longtime Bond custodians Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli in February 2025, four years after No Time to Die was released. Now, Pattinson will tux up as the seventh cinematic Bond under the stewardship of super-producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal and the vision of GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, marking arguably the biggest role of the 40-year-old London-born actor’s career.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Rumors of Pattinson’s selection caught fire in October, when delays on The Batman Part II gave him a window to audition for Bond at Berkshire’s Bray Studios, alongside peers Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden, and an unnamed fourth actor. The chatter heightened a couple weeks later when various British tabloids suggested that Turner, O’Connor, and Lowden were each the preferred choice to satisfy the demands and responsibilities of the beloved British action hero—heightening suspicion that a final decision was looming. According to THR, the finalists were judged “based on stunts, camera presence.” But Pattinson’s last-minute arrival clearly tipped the scale.

“Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007,” said Villeneuve in a statement to THR. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

It’s both a particularly inspired and obvious choice. Pattinson’s physical traits and characteristics hue close to Ian Fleming’s original Bond—tall and slim, with dark hair. He’s already a bona fide movie star, the current face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise; meanwhile, the selection catches him at the tail end of another booked-and-busy year. Unlike his auditioning peers, the acclaimed actor will enter the franchise well-experienced working in IP and with big-name directors. After co-leading this spring’s The Drama, he chewed up scenes as Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey (the second time working with Nolan after Tenet), made a creepy turn as Chris Hansen in Primetime, and will close 2026 as Scytale in Dune: Part 3—now the first of future Villeneuve collaborations, a relationship that surely helped him acquire his license to kill.

“James Bond is one of the most beloved, inspiring, iconic, and yet enigmatic characters in literature and movies,” Pascal and Heyman stated jointly to THR. “The legacy of this character is in great hands with Robert Pattinson. His fearlessness as an actor, his self-deprecating wit, and his ability to continually reinvent himself make him the perfect Bond for our times.”

The decision to hire a movie star isn’t a risky choice, but there’s not much precedent within the franchise—especially recently. When he succeeded Pierce Brosnan as Bond in 2005, beating out Clive Owen, Michael Fassbender, and Henry Cavill, Craig boasted an under-the-radar resume. He’d just come off Matthew Vaughn’s crime thriller Layer Cake, but otherwise had played supporting roles in Road to Perdition, The Mother, and Enduring Love. His only big-budget studio experience came several years earlier as Angelina Jolie’s love interest in Tomb Raider.

Naturally, the British press drew its fangs upon his selection, critiquing everything from his general obscurity to his physical features, which stood in stark contrast to previous Bond actors. “The Mane’s Blond, James Blond,” chirped The Irish Times, while The London Daily Mirror played with the same pun: “The Name’s Bland … James Bland.” At his official introduction to the press along the Thames, Craig arrived on a speedboat wearing a life vest, attracting instant mockery—the first of several digs about his less-than-sleek aesthetic and physical abilities. (One tabloid insulted an on-set sunburn and his inability to drive a stick shift car.)

Pattinson, however, has mostly conjured genuine excitement—not in spite of, but because of, his extreme familiarity with moviegoers, dating back to his Young Adult days in the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises. Since then, over the last decade-plus, his eccentric characters and commanding screen presence immediately qualifies him as someone “stirring and exciting and different,” descriptors that Pascal said she prioritized in their methodical search.

Thanks to director Martin Campbell, Casino Royale returned the Bond franchise to earth and established Craig as a grounded, gritty action star in the mold of Jason Bourne. The movie ended up raking in $616 million globally, the highest earning Bond film to date, and launched Craig into four more sequels. Similarly, Pattinson will have the benefit of a highly-respected, Oscar-nominated director in his corner with experience shepherding IP into new places and eliciting compelling performances about tortured male protagonists.

With Villeneuve at the helm of this 26th installment, don’t expect another hard creative pivot; the man behind Prisoners, Blade Runner 2049, and Dune wasn’t hired to bring back the colorful, absurdist, gadget-heavy era that Austin Powers parodied throughout the 90’s. Still, new leadership means a new direction—a clean slate for Pattinson to burnish an already diverse, robust career and prove his chops again at the highest level of scrutiny.

#6580. French Onion Croissant Strata

A breakfast strata is one of our go-tos when we want a hearty, shareable brunch dish, but it’s hard to put into words how good this French onion croissant strata is. It takes a few extra minutes to deeply caramelize the onions, but the extra flavor and richness make a HUGE difference.

Making it French Onion:Caramelizing the onions over medium heat helps them brown evenly and consistently. If the onions begin to stick or burn, add a splash of water to bring them back! Garlic, thyme, and black pepper are the aromatic unsung heroes in the onions, so you don’t want to skip them. Deglazing with white wine is essential in any French onion recipe, so use the one you’d sip! Once the wine has reduced, add some beef stock to impart meaty French onion soup flavor. The caramelized onions then get layered with torn croissants and Gruyère cheese, and topped with dollops of cream cheese.

Delish Official:Eggland's Best Eggs are the Official Eggs of Delish. That means they're the only eggs we're using in our recipe content.

Storage:The beautiful thing about a breakfast strata is that you can make it ahead. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 day and reheat until the internal temperature reaches 165°. This is also great to portion and store for breakfast at the office.

#6578. Luminous Holiday Eye Looks That Shine All Season

Whether you go for gilded lids, jewel-toned liners, or a vibrant wash of color, you can find your next party-ready eye look at Ulta Beauty.

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The holiday party circuit requires a shift in your beauty wardrobe—especially when it comes to eyes. Think softly smoked bronze lids, flashes of metallic gold shadow, and jewel-toned eyeliner that makes even your go-to little black dress feel entirely new. Festive gatherings are the perfect opportunity to try something outside your usual makeup routine, whether that means trading black eyeliner for emerald green or adding a touch of gold to an otherwise understated eye. And with the right products, you don't need a makeup artist's skills to pull it off.

From versatile shadow palettes to long-wearing liners, Ulta Beauty's prestige makeup selection offers endless ways to play with color and texture, whether you're dressing for an intimate dinner or going all out for New Year's Eve.

Below, 4 fail-safe strategies to sparkle on your next night out.

Unlike a traditional black smoky eye, which can sometimes feel a little severe, bronze brings warmth and definition while keeping the overall effect more understated. Charlotte Tilbury's Hollywood Instant Look in a Palette takes much of the guesswork out of choosing complementary colors, with three eyeshadows and a selection of complexion powders in one place. To create a soft, bronze smoky eye, sweep the lightest eyeshadow across your lids, blend the deeper shade into the crease, and tap a little shimmer onto the center to catch the light. Finish with the included bronzer and blush to bring some warmth to the rest of your face.

For an even simpler, more minimal approach, the Polite Society Dual Intentions Eyeshadow Duo pairs two complementary shades. Concentrate the darker color along your upper lash line before blending it outward for that slightly undone, smoky finish.

The most sophisticated way to incorporate jewel tones into your holiday eye makeup is to swap your usual black eyeliner or mascara for a rich, saturated color. Emerald green, sapphire blue, and amethyst purple can make even the simplest makeup feel a little more interesting, especially when paired with an otherwise neutral face. If you're hesitant to go too bright, deeper shades like midnight blue offer a less dramatic departure from black.

Whether you're drawing a thin line along your lashes or going for a bold, dramatic wing, Anastasia Beverly Hills DramaLine Longwear Waterproof Gel Eyeliner Pencil glides on as smoothly as a gel eyeliner, but is just as easy to use as a pencil. It comes in colors ranging from metallic purple to emerald green; use it to draw a sharp, colorful wing or keep the pigment close to your lashline for just a hint of something unexpected.

Mascara is another way to try out color without committing to a full eye look. Tarte Tartelette Tubing Mascara comes in statement-making hues that give lashes a little personality of their own. Try pairing a vibrant magenta with neutral eyeshadow to let your lashes take center stage, or match your mascara to your eyeliner for a coordinated, monochromatic effect. The tubing formula resists smudging and flaking throughout the evening, then comes off with warm water when it's time to wash your face.

For an effortless metallic gold eye, focus the color on the center of your lids or the inner corners, where it naturally catches the light. You don't need to cover your entire eyelid in glitter to make an impression; these carefully placed touches of gold can feel just as striking, particularly with an otherwise pared-back makeup look.

For a delicate, gilded finish, start with a gold or champagne shade from the Ulta Beauty Collection Eyeshadow Singles. Use a fluffy brush to diffuse the color across your lids, or press it on with your fingertip for a more intense, saturated effect. The single-pan format is convenient for slipping into your makeup bag should your after-work plans call for a quick change of pace.

To balance the warmth of gold eyeshadow, consider brown mascara instead of your usual black. The Hourglass Unlocked Instant Extensions Mascara Duo includes both Espresso and Black, giving you the option to keep your lashes understated or add a little more contrast. Espresso pairs well with champagne and bronze tones, defining lashes without overpowering the rest of your eye makeup. Whichever color you choose, the tubing formula creates length and separation while helping prevent smudges.

The best holiday eye makeup gift sets offer a mix of versatile neutrals, richer statement colors, and different finishes, so there's room to test out new styles without needing an entire makeup collection. Palettes that combine mattes and metallics are useful, since they can take someone from an understated daytime eye to a more dramatic look for evening.

For someone who enjoys changing up their makeup for different occasions, the Tarte You Know You Love Me Collector's Set offers plenty of options. It includes two mini Amazonian Clay eyeshadow palettes—one with warm golden shades for glamorous precious-metal-inspired eyes and another with cool rosy neutrals for a more subtle, romantic take—plus two mascaras and two lip products to top things off.

If a streamlined makeup routine is your holiday wish, Morphe Sky's the Limit Face & Eye Palette brings together coordinating rose-gold and mauve tones for eyes and cheeks. The mix of matte and shimmery eyeshadows makes it easy to adjust the intensity depending on the occasion, and the fact that the kit comes with blush, cheek balms, and setting powder means you won't have to reach for several other products to complete your makeup.
