#6534. Joaquin Phoenix Wasn’t Thinking About 'Her' When He Filmed This Intelligent Eyewear Campaign

It feels like a scene out of a sci-fi movie: Joaquin Phoenix is standing across from me, instructing me to speak into his eyeglasses in a foreign language.

“Let’s see what happens,” the Oscar winner says. “It could be any language.”

The idea we’re testing here is whether the glasses Phoenix is wearing—a dark-rimmed pair from the South Korean luxury eyewear brand Gentle Monster’s new Intelligent Eyewear collection—could live-translate these words into English. This is one of the glasses’ capabilities the actor was most delighted to discover while he was shooting their campaign film directed by another Oscar winner, Jonathan Glazer. The glasses were crafted in partnership with Google and Samsung, and feature AI-powered technology.

Joaquin Phoenix in the Jonathan Glazer-directed campaign spot.

The last time Phoenix appeared in a fashion campaign, it was 1997 and he was modeling moody suits for Prada. This time around, he stars in the Glazer-directed spot that Phoenix says was partially inspired by the 1969 documentary Salesman, in which vendors travel across New England selling Bibles. In the Gentle Monster ad, Phoenix’s character—who has an intense, quasi-manic energy—ventures into an unnamed hotel, where he falls into a deep sleep and meets colorful, large creatures at the end of a hallway. (One might even call them…Gentle Monsters.) Per a press release, the “intelligent eyewear becomes his way of understanding their language and communicating with them, opening up unexpected possibilities for connection.”

Phoenix had wanted to work with Glazer for a long time. “I’ve known him for years, and when we all approached him, we came up with this really interesting and offbeat idea that just [had so] much mood. He just gets super excited and inspired,” the actor says. During the shoot, the Zone of Interest filmmaker kept the camera rolling for prolonged periods of time, encouraging Phoenix to harness different emotions. A moment in the ad might last for “30 seconds, but we shot for 15 minutes,” he explains. “A whole range of things are happening in those 15 minutes, things that we were trying.”

In an email, Glazer reiterated that he was glad to have had a reason to work with Phoenix: “The first image I had was him asleep, maybe dreaming, with the glasses all wonky across his face. The rest kind of grew from there,” the director said.

When I meet the actor last Wednesday at 23 Wall Street in Manhattan—where Gentle Monster has staged an enormous activation for the Intelligent Eyewear launch, complete with fake horses with wagging tails and huge surreal sculptures—it’s hard not to think about his turn in the 2013 film Her, one of the most prophetic AI movies of our time. In the Spike Jonze near-future drama, Phoenix’s character, Theodore Twombly, chats with and subsequently falls for an AI-powered operating system voiced by Scarlett Johansson. If 2011’s Contagion foreshadowed the COVID-19 pandemic, Her’s depiction of chatbots feels eerily similar to the world of ChatGPT dots, Meta Muses, Claude Duets, and Gemini Sparks that we’re beginning to grow accustomed to.

Phoenix and his partner, actress Rooney Mara, wearing Intelligent Eyewear at the Gentle Monster event in Manhattan.

When I ask Phoenix if filming the campaign made him think of Her, he shrugs. “I wasn’t. It seems like I should have,” he says. “It’s funny because I think that sometimes films have more of, maybe, an impact on the people that view them than for me, but I hadn’t thought about that. Somebody just made a joke about it actually, and I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re right.’”

Phoenix, who most recently starred in 2025’s politically tinged neo-Western Eddington, leaves on his Intelligent Eyewear glasses—which are Gemini-embedded, sleek, and thick-rimmed—while we speak.

“The thing is,” he says, “I’m not even aware that I’m wearing them.”

#6533. Grace Cacciato Wins the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final

After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final. A panel of judges selected her roasted squab with chanterelle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat, black raspberry, and Swiss chard purées to represent the United States at the Grand Finale in Milan.

The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City on Monday, and the winner was announced the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024–25 US winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, DC, and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

Representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in New York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

Saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he said. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

The chefs had five hours to prepare and execute their signature dishes in the Test Kitchen. With an hour remaining, guests had the opportunity to mingle over food and drinks. Chef Rachel Bindel, a 2022 US Finalist, served rye toast piled high with Maryland blue crab, horseradish crème, and pickled green tomato. Chef Akshay Kumar, a 2024 finalist, tucked Kumamoto oysters into a pani puri with cucumber gel and lemon foam. Tomato pie from Philadelphia’s Pizza Freak Co., spoonfuls of Petrossian caviar, and a selection of wines, S.Pellegrino beverages, and cocktails rounded out the reception.

Nilou Motamed, a culinary expert and Iron Chef judge on Netflix, hosted the competition. Accomplished chefs from several states served as judges: chef and co-owner E.J. Lagasse of Emeril’s in New Orleans; executive chef and partner Fariyal Abdullahi of Hav & Mar in New York City; Isabel Coss, executive chef at Pascual and founding pastry chef at Lutèce in Washington, DC; Jon Yao, head chef and owner at Kato in Los Angeles; and Ryan Ratino, executive chef and owner at Bresca and Jônt in Washington, DC.

Motamed explained that each competitor had spent several months developing their dish alongside a chef mentor. The mentors were in the Test Kitchen throughout the competition, but were not permitted to participate in the cooking. She also outlined the three pillars of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy: Community, Competition, and Mentorship, which support its mission to discover and nurture the next generation of culinary talent.

Each chef’s arrival was announced by a burst of music and a live video feed from the Test Kitchen, where a fleet of servers collected the finished plates before delivering them to the judges. First up was chef Adolfo Pucci of Michelin-starred Ariete in Miami. His dish, “Three Shores, One Table,” told the story of his Venezuelan heritage, his family’s roots in Southern Italy, and his current home in Miami. The ambitious plate featured a lamb ragù inspired by his grandmother’s cooking and lacto-fermented Florida blueberries.

Chef Amit Kumar of three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park in New York City presented the competition’s only fully vegan dish: “Sunchoke with Banana Blossoms, Chanterelles, and Sherry.” Drawing on memories of the banana trees he grew up with in India, Kumar combined banana blossoms, sunchoke purée, chanterelle mushrooms, and a ragù of sherry and banana flowers to create a hearty and deeply satisfying dish. Judge Fariyal Abdullahi called it “a very successful dish, not just a very successful vegan dish.”

Representing Auro at Four Seasons Resort and Residences Napa Valley, chef Evan Neumann presented “From the Valley to the Shoreline,” a love letter to the terroir of Northern California and Provence, where he grew up. Kombu-poached wild razor clams mingled with Napa verjuice and coastal seaweeds in a dish the judges found exceptionally creative. Neumann took home the S.Pellegrino Social Responsibility Award for his thoughtful approach to social responsibility and sustainable practices.

At just 21, chef Lucy Field of New York City’s fine dining bastion Per Se was the youngest competitor. Her dish, “Pekin Duck, Cherry, Plum,” was a study in restraint with only six components.

Chef Marcus Osorio, chef de cuisine at Living Room in Los Angeles, drew inspiration from his Salvadoran and Indigenous roots for his “Tamal de Pollo.” The dish featured corn sourced from Somos Maíz, the company founded by his mentor, chef Ron Oliver, and a mole poblano the two developed together. Judge Isabel Coss noted the challenge of preparing a mole with such limited time, but the judges were impressed by Osorio’s ability to marry European cooking techniques with soulful Indigenous ingredients and flavors.

Chef Nickolas Abbott hails from the small Appalachian town of Waynesville, North Carolina, and leads Chop Shop Butchery in Asheville. At the competition, he told the story of his community on a plate. His “Smoked Pork Loin, Fennel & Cheese Slaw, Sweet Potato, Asparagus, Fried Sausage, Pork Sauce Robert” reflected the people who shaped him, particularly his grandmother, his greatest inspiration as a chef.

Los Angeles–based chef Natasha Daniels of Providence showcased her vegetable-forward, zero-waste approach with “The Whole Bird, The Whole Garden.” The dish incorporated every part of a chicken across four preparations, alongside an array of vegetables and herbs inspired by her time working at The Chef’s Garden.

Daniels received two honors: the Acqua Panna Connection in Gastronomy Award and the Fine Dining Lovers Award. Voted on by regional mentors, the Acqua Panna award recognized the dish that best demonstrated a connection between culinary traditions. Daniels’s approach also resonated with Fine Dining Lovers insiders, who selected her for their award that honors “a chef’s expression of personal belief.”

With only minutes to spare, chef Nicolas Lopez of 888 in Nashville arrived with “Pozole or Chawanmushi…?” Combining pozole, corn, and langoustine, Lopez connected his upbringing in Mexico with a culinary journey that has been shaped by Scandinavian ingredients and Japanese techniques. Although the judges could have used more time to explore the dish, they were intrigued by his influences and impressed by his technique.

The final competitor, Juwon Lee, is the chef of Octavia in San Francisco. Lee was born in South Korea and grew up in Singapore before making California his home. His dish, “Curry and Quail with Ingredients My Mother Said Were Healthy,” drew on memories of eating Indonesian fried chicken and his mother’s insistence on including vegetables at family dinners. “I believe in the term happy food,” Lee explained. “There are no restrictions other than bringing joy to the eater and the chef.”

Congratulations to all 10 chefs who competed, and best of luck to Chef Cacciato as she continues to work with her mentor and prepares to represent the United States at the 2027 Grand Finale in Milan. Follow her journey at @sanpellegrino_us.

#6532. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6530. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6528. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6527. David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

One of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

#6526. Andy Baraghani's Ditto Café Is His Most Personal Project Yet

Andy Baraghani is more afraid of becoming stagnant than he is of dying. Stagnancy, he’s quick to clarify, is different from stillness. Stagnancy is like a fetid pond; stillness is meditative. Baraghani seems to be at risk of neither.

It is late morning on the first actually chilly day of autumn and we are staring one another down across a stainless-steel prep table, which has been dragooned into use as an island in his outrageously good-looking kitchen. He is about to make me scones—salty-sweet ones with dates and lemon zest, an offering under development for his forthcoming café Ditto. But first, we’ll need to pop out for cream.

Quite literally in motion since I arrived, Baraghani finishes his point on stagnancy: He fears a life in which he is not learning, moving, or evolving “as a writer, a cook, and a good gay,” he says.

He lives just a few blocks from the Union Square Greenmarket, where niche pepper varieties are currently splayed in colorful fractals across folding tables. We have just completed a ground floor tour of the apartment that the chef-cum-writer-cum-chef shares with his husband, Keith Pollock. Now he moves across the kitchen and pauses at the Crittall-style window. It gives me 30 seconds to take inventory of his countertop alliums.

These details feel important. Baraghani has become a sort of standard-bearer for exquisite seasonal produce and the exquisite life one can lead preparing such stuff. I clock a couple of shallots, which sit in a Swid Powell bowl beside five heirloom tomatoes. It occurs to me that even onions are more beautiful in Baraghani’s universe.

“Oh,” he says casually, following my gaze. “Torpedo shallots.” As if all of our countertops look like this.

In the decade or so since he became a household name for a certain set of a certain era (food-obsessed aesthetes who love an acidic drizzle and a hard, salty cheese), as a video star for a certain magazine—okay, this one—his fandom has only continued to explode.

His debut cookbook, The Cook You Want to Be, was a New York Times bestseller and the recipient of a James Beard Award. He has more than 370,000 followers across Instagram and TikTok. He’s been called “the Internet boyfriend of our dreams.” Vogue covered his wedding. The New York Times published his ideal Thanksgiving menu. In the last 24 hours alone, Baraghani has been busy beating out creative director Terrence O’Connor for a Best Body prize at the podcast How Long Gone’s inaugural “Goneies” Award Show, (Baraghani was asked to remove his blazer to reveal a formfitting Dario Vitale–era Versace pink tank top) before running into David Tanis while shopping for groceries.

When Baraghani announced he would be opening a restaurant this fall near Union Square with restaurateur Michael Silber, publications began tripping over themselves to cover the news. Still, he says, few have pushed him on the true meaning of the name Ditto. Perhaps they were too busy trying to keep up.

Baraghani takes a seat on one of the iron stools beside the prep table and there is a rare, brief silence, which is broken almost immediately by the tinny opening notes of a techno song emanating from the crew performing a renovation on the lower floor. I inquire about his cortisol levels as he juggles opening Ditto a few blocks away, the second cookbook he has just shot in this apartment, and now the remodel below us.

Baraghani grins. “I feel calm,” he insists. “If something goes wrong, I can fix it, because I feel pretty clear on what I want to achieve.”

He has spent the last 10 years peppering his recipes with caveats. “I know that my food may be a touch too lemony for some,” he writes in The Cook You Want To Be. “And that I use what has been called a ridiculous amount of herbs.”

His background too. Years ago, he penned an essay for this magazine about growing up Iranian in a post-9/11 America; he started to go by Andy instead of Andisheh and bought an “Italian Stallion” T-shirt. He wrote about learning to accept his sexuality in restaurant kitchens, where he rarely encountered other gay men, and in his family life. He grew up in the Bay Area, the son of parents who had emigrated from Iran to Berkeley in 1977. The piece ended with an admission: “So as nice as it would be for this story to end with that Iran feature or getting my dream job at Bon Appétit, the truth is that I’m still trying to figure things out. It’s not always steady progress.”

Since I had a baby six weeks ago, I have been walking around floored that the adults in my life could have ever been children, but with Andy, I don’t have to work too hard to picture it. He has a particularly cheerful sense of wonder. When I ask about it, he says it comes from his upbringing. His parents were political activists. Andy’s mother worked as an aesthetician (yes, he established his famous skin-care routine early). He grew up surrounded by a diverse community of immigrants who would invite his family to their celebrations and into their homes, where a young Baraghani got to taste dishes from far-flung places. After he landed in New York, he would take respite in stints abroad, traveling from hostel to hostel so he could eat his way across Vietnam, Lebanon, and Turkey.

Now, though, Baraghani says he is done footnoting his vision. In the intervening years since that essay, Baraghani has written and cooked and tasted at warp speed. He was bound to self-actualize in the same timeframe it took the rest of us to figure out how to style barrel-leg pants. Or perhaps it’s the reality of having to reckon with what he can’t change: In 2024, after a battle with small-cell lung cancer, his beloved father passed away. Baraghani tells me that before it was stagnancy, his greatest fear was losing a parent. He has since learned that loss isn’t something to solve, but a tremendous void one must learn to live with.

“There’s an explicit confidence you’ll see [at Ditto,]” he says. The dishes will weave together all of the threads of Baraghani-ism: seasonal vegetables prepared deftly with Persian flourishes, blending tart and sour and aromatic with a firm point-of-view. If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.)

Literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in New York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with plans for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

The goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was important for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the plan is breakfast and lunch.

Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

The sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.)

Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

As we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he says simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

Later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

And for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

#6525. Nike Made an Air Jordan 1 for Guys Who Love Japanese Denim

Menswear guys love Japanese denim. Menswear guys also love sneakers. So why not make some kicks for the people who can tell you exactly which artisanal mill produced their selvedge? That seems to be the thinking behind the new Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko.’

Social Status is a North Carolina-based sneaker and streetwear boutique owned by the Whitaker Group, the same company behind A Ma Maniére. Over the years, it’s worked with Nike on everything from milk-inspired Dunks to Air Pennys. The shop’s last proper Jordan collab was an extremely hairy Air Jordan 6 from 2019, but now the pair are back with something a little easier to wear.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’

Social Status’s take on the AJ1 Low starts with the classic ‘Chicago’ color palette. The toebox is white, the overlays are red, and the Swoosh and collar are black. But rather than keeping everything box-fresh, Social Status has roughed up the leather so it arrives pre-scuffed, as though you’ve owned these shoes for years.

The big switch happens across the sidewalls. The usual white leather panels have been replaced with mismatched patches of indigo fabric covered in white sashiko-style stitching. Sashiko is a traditional Japanese embroidery technique used to reinforce, repair, and extend the life of clothing. It’s particularly associated with vintage workwear and denim, which is why these Jordans look like they’ve been mended using a very expensive pair of jeans.

There’s also an old-school nylon tongue, a slightly aged sole, and a custom shoebox wrapped in the same blue pattern.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’

While you might normally expect this sort of big Jordan release to land on the High, it’s nice to see the Low silhouette get some love. Some dudes prefer it, after all—it’s less bulky around the ankle and works better under wider trousers. You still get all the bits that make an Air Jordan 1 instantly recognizable, only without half the collar.

The Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’ is set to drop on December 18 for $155 through Social Status, with a wider release via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists expected to arrive later on. Japanese denim guys, get your credit cards ready.

#6524. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

His much-anticipated film, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, finally comes out this week. Zada and I spoke the morning of his New York City premiere, while he was being shuttled from one press obligation to the next, already go-go-go before actually hitting the red carpet Monday night in custom Louis Vuitton, punctuated with a pair of gold-toed cowboy boots from Pharrell’s first collection for the brand.

In the film, Zada plays a young Haymitch Abernathy, who we follow through his own Hunger Games, some twenty-five years ahead of the events of the original trilogy. When asked about the movie, the 21-year-old Australian demonstrates palpable care and excitement, even a bit of sadness that it’s over. “I just think that it was the most I’ve had to prepare and the most support that I’ve had and the most that I’ve ever stepped into a character’s shoes,” Zada says. “And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.”

Since being cast, he’s barely had a second to stop and reflect on joining one of the biggest franchises in the world—and this comes right on the heels of East of Eden, too, in which Zada played another haunted young man. He laughs when I note the comparison: “I guess I just pride myself on my ability to show my vulnerability.”

Below, read our full conversation with the emerging star as he reflects on his Hunger Games journey, talks red carpet style, and shares his thoughts on Robert Pattinson playing James Bond.

Joseph Zada: Yeah, I wonder if I’ll be nervous.

Maybe towards the start. It doesn’t get old… but it gets familiar.

Well, I did SiriusXM this morning, and then, I mean, it’s basically just been like, "Hey, do press all day and then go to your premiere." So there’s not much time for a ritual, so I guess I go a little bit nonverbal and half-dissociate.

No, it’s so much fun. I have a lot of fun at these premieres. It’s always like a crazy, crazy crowd. It’s always crazy to see this many fans and the passion they have for this project. I mean, it’s not every day that you get to step into something with a built-in fan base where people are already coming out and supporting it before they’ve even seen it. Where did I have the most fun? I had a lot of fun in London because my little sister was there, my little sister and my brother’s girlfriend, so I got to hang out with them and I haven’t seen them in a while. And Mexico. Mexico was the craziest event that we’ve had. There were literally thousands, several thousands of people there. The reception was incredible.

Am I allowed to drop this? Oh, yes, that is what this [interview] is for. I’m wearing a Louis Vuitton suit—custom, custom—that Jason [Bolden] and I have worked together on, and I’m a big fan of the boots. The boots are pretty dope.

I feel a lot more comfortable in these clothes nowadays, and it’s actually become a lot more enjoyable to put them on. And it feels like more of an armor and less of a scary thing, and it feels like I build a lot of confidence being able to do this.

My red carpet style, I think... I don’t know. Just whatever Jason puts me in for the night.

Yeah, I think just doing it so often and finding different looks and just being able to wear all the different brands and find what I’m comfortable in.

I think as a young man, that’s what I find interesting in these performances of these young men coming of age, and I think that was really what I was just looking for in my early career. I love being able to portray that in my performances.

And it was just such a joy to act in this and to feel what it was like to really be this character.

I did just see the Bond casting news! I am chuffed. That is so exciting. That is beyond exciting. He is just the most phenomenal actor, and he really just makes the most interesting choices. And I think him in that role, the stoicism that he’ll bring along with those really interesting choices, it’s going to make that character so interesting. He’s a really special actor. #6522. Maple Pumpkin Overnight Oats

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.)

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

#6521. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6520. Robert Pattinson, I’m Begging You For a Quirked-Up James Bond

Our long international nightmare is finally over: two-time Meme of the Year nominee Robert Pattinson has been chosen as Daniel Craig’s James Bond successor, bringing an end to an exhausting series of “reports” and “leaks” about Amazon’s search for a new 007. Finally we can stop the debates and fan-casting and let Patts and Denis Villeneuve cook until they’re ready to present their new vision. But that would require a level of restraint that the internet doesn’t typically exercise. Immediately after the protracted process of casting Bond concluded, the internet moved on to naming its dream picks for Bond Girls and Bond Villains (sometimes, to brilliant effect.) I can’t say I have a dog in either fight, at least not right now. My Bond WishList is of a different magnitude altogether: can we make James Bond silly again? Just a little, even, 15 percent goofball?

In the hands of another (read: more limited) actor, I’d never suggest such a risky swerve. But the best thing about Pattinson is his range. Sure, if Villeneuve and co. want to render Bond as the stoic and taciturn gentleman he’s generally been this century, Rob has proven he can do that, as every Tenet truther has been gleefully preaching for the last 24 hours. But more often than not, Pattinson is keen to get weird, whether that’s going Full Freak, as he does in Primetime, or approaching certain archetypal parts with a silly, goofy mood (like his conniving suitor in The Odyssey). He can do a “voice” (Mickey 17), he can do scumbag grime (Good Time), he can do hapless screwball (The Drama). Why not make what’ll be his biggest role to date a little cocktail of all his best elements? (Okay, he can leave the Mickey 17 voice behind.)

20 years ago, Casino Royale was a refreshing reset and a crucial corrective to the overflowing ridiculousness of the Piece Brosnan era. But in the past two decades, the pendulum has swung back—the gritty reboot has become studios' stock-in-trade. I feel the same way about Batman; the actual risky choice would be to make something less like Nolan’s series that, instead, hewed a little closer to, say, Batman Forever, or even the gothic camp of Tim Burton’s two films.

Of course, Robert Pattinson was at the center of a Batman reboot as well, and the result was a movie that felt more like a spiritual cousin to David Fincher’s Se7en; audiences ate it up so much that the hunger for a sequel persists even after endless delays. When it comes to franchises as high-stakes as Batman or Bond, you can’t trust these increasingly sauceless execs to make anything but the basic choice. There’s no reason to expect Jeff Bezos isn’t texting Denis screenshots from Skyfall for reference from his megayacht at this very moment.

But if there’s anybody capable of putting a little English on the handle while still giving the mainstream what it wants, it’s Big Bob Pattinson. He could easily make his James Bond a little off, or he could go full seductive cad who smiles like Neil Tenet, has a ki with Q, and charms women with some playful banter instead of simply brooding them into submission. I’m not looking for invisible cars and sharks with lasers, or a Lothario like Roger Moore who speaks in puns. All I’m asking is that we give camp a chance. Because ultimately, the most exciting thing Villeneuve and Pattinson can do to set their Bond apart would be to loosen him up a little.

#6519. 23 Healthy Breakfasts That'll Keep You Full Till Lunch

When it comes to healthy breakfasts, free yourself to eat more than plain yogurt and granola bars. And honestly, those $19 acai bowls from the smoothie shop aren’t that nutritious. A truly healthy breakfast has plenty of carbs for energy (this includes fiber-rich ingredients like whole grains, berries, legumes, and seeds); muscle-and-bone-supporting protein; and plenty of healthy fats for nutrient absorption. Many of these recipes can easily be made ahead and doled out from the freezer, so before you swing by the drive-through for bland egg muffins, consider these more flavorful options. Here are 23 of our favorite healthy breakfasts.

When it comes to healthy breakfast ideas, my mind immediately goes to oats. Also chia seed pudding. So the newest edition of my column Good for You is a chia seed–overnight oat hybrid, which also uses up a can of pumpkin purée (I bet you have one in the pantry).

Frozen or fresh berries work great in these accidentally vegan pancakes (thanks, silken tofu!) from Good for You. A good drizzle of maple syrup is all they need for accompaniment, but since I’m not vegan, I enjoy them with a swipe of Greek yogurt.

Another Good for You hit is this speedy, protein-and-collagen-rich soup, which is something in between Italian stracciatella and Chinese egg drop soup.

Okay, after this one, I’ll stop shamelessly promoting my column. But seriously, don’t sleep on this hydrating mixed berry smoothie, especially if you’re lukewarm on eating plain cottage cheese.

This tricked out avocado toast is loaded with hot smoked salmon and creamy scrambled eggs.

You maybe haven’t seen an omelet filled with sliced apple and cheddar, but I recommend trying before knocking.

Oatmeal is an ideal choice in the morning for carbs and fiber. I like to slowly stir in egg whites while it’s simmering on the stove for extra protein and top it with ground flaxseed.

A great option for weekend mornings. You could top it with feta or yogurt, dunk whole wheat toast in the sauce, or spoon it over rice, anything goes.

Nothing hits quite like a breakfast burrito, but I can’t buy one every day and still pay rent. DIY to the rescue: I line the tortilla with salsa or hot sauce and sometimes add leftover refried beans if I have them.

The texture of chia seed pudding took me some time to get used to, but now I’m obsessed. Strange how the body adapts! I love that this recipe makes enough for a workweek of breakfasts. Head here for our favorite matcha powders.

If you don’t have time to make the hot honey mixture, these simple breakfast tacos are great with any hot sauces or chile-based condiments that happen to be in the fridge.

This Persian egg dish is similar to a frittata, which means it makes for great meal prep. It takes awhile to wash all the herbs, so make sure you have time, but leftovers will last a few days in the fridge. I like it cold with a swipe of Greek yogurt, but you do you.

Meet the bran muffins you’ll actually crave. Squidgy dates and chopped chocolate make these more like a hearty breakfast cake than the dense pucks you may have eaten in the past.

If it’s not heirloom tomato season, opt for smaller cherry or Campari tomatoes in this recipe—your taste buds will thank you.

To bulk up this green smoothie into a filling meal, add some nut butter and cottage cheese or plain yogurt, plus a scoop of protein powder if you have it.

Leftover cooked quinoa mocking you in the fridge? Stir it in to these blueberry muffins. Win-win.

Speaking of leftover quinoa, if you’re looking for a savory option instead of sweet, throw together this morning salad with a few boiled eggs and smoked trout.

While I personally love mushy porridge, I understand that cakey is a more pleasant texture for many. If that’s the case for you, baked oatmeal is the solution.

Serving brunch to a crowd? Make this breakfast casserole. Just grab a nice loaf of sourdough to slice alongside.

If you haven’t yet tried fried eggs that were based with turmeric oil, now is your moment.

For the savory oatmeal fans out there, try simmering with instant dashi powder and salt-softened vegetables.

A homemade gluten-free loaf that you’ll dream about. Try it with butter and a slice of aged cheese like cheddar or cream cheese and smoked fish.

#6518. Upgrade Your Basics: Best Undershirts for Men in 2026

Just because you don't see a building's foundation doesn't mean it isn't holding everything up. In much the same way, the best undershirts for men are the humble base layer of countless great outfits. Many GQ staffers, in fact, wear-test theirs daily, and yet they're often overlooked, even though they've long-perfected their role: to be the protective layer between your gross body and your steezy, attention-hungry shirts and polos.

And while they're certainly good for some added warmth in the winter, there's a common misconception that they can make the wearer too hot. In fact, lightweight, moisture-wicking undershirts made from fabrics like modal, or cotton blends can actually transfer the sweat away from your body, speeding up your cooling down. All that's to say: Undershirts are more than just men’s underwear. They’re the cornerstone of a hall-of-fame fit.

An undershirt is an undershirt is an undershirt. If you want the most straightforward version, the kind that you’re picturing in your head is most likely from Calvin Klein. It’s a classic crewneck undershirt that’s made of a lightweight jersey that’s 100% cotton which has a smooth, very slightly brushed hand that feels worn-in in the best way possible. The slim fit won’t cause any weird bunching or bulging and it’s got enough length to stay tucked even when you’re out on the town cutting rugs.

My colleague, GQ senior commerce editor Avidan Grossman, has been wearing CK's genre-defining undershirts since his high school years. (He could do without the logo at the hem, but has made his peace with it, given that you never see it once it's tucked.) Otherwise, he prizes Calvin Klein's riff for its simple, pared-down design and blessed lack of modern-day frills. After all, not every shirt needs to moisture wick or odor block. If you just want an undershirt that gets the job done, don't overthink it.

Sometimes, sleeves are just too much undershirt. That’s where tanks come in. Also known as A-shirts, the humble, sleeveless tank has been rocked by every heartthrob and neighborhood grandpa as far back as anyone can remember. And while the low neck and lack of sleeves means you’ll practically never see them underneath a button-up, the irony is that they look great shown off with an unbuttoned camp shirt or on their own.

For the money, we think Hanes takes the cake with their multipack of undershirts. The stretchy ribbed jersey is made of 100% cotton and fits snug with a low neck that’s slightly squared off compared to most tanks. They may cost just under twenty bucks for a pack of six, but they look like a million bucks. “I’ve had buyer's remorse over many a menswear garment over the years,” explains GQ editor Jordan Bowman, "but the one thing that has never let me down is the humble tank top from Hanes. They nailed the fit and the material, and the great thing is, you can buy a pack just about anywhere."

If every part of your wardrobe has to be fit for a king, down to the most basics of basics, then CDLP is what we’d recommend, my liege. The reality is that most luxury tees don’t offer much more than the regular stuff. It’s diminishing returns after a certain price point, but CDLP is the notable exception. My colleague, our contributing editor Louis Cheslaw, has put his same CDLP cottons through the ringer year after year, and says they still haven't lost their luster.

It’s a pricey undershirt, for sure, but the high-quality fabric has a silky hand and lightweight feel that’s unparalleled. (It really feels like you’re almost wearing nothing.) Thanks to a wider neckline, you’re a lot less likely to see the tee poking out, too. And if you feel like such a nice T-shirt is wasted as underwear, don’t worry—the cut and shorter length means it looks great untucked, and can double as your regular T-shirt too.

Mack Weldon’s silver series of garments is what happens when you get nerdy about chemistry and fashion (in the best possible way). The Ionic+ technology embeds silver charged silver ions which are naturally antimicrobial into the fabric itself. Essentially, that means bacteria and odor is neutralized, which means you can take it easy on the deodorant. Beyond that, the tees are made of super long staple Supima cotton and a smidge of lycra for an extra silky fee, comfortable stretch, and long-lasting wear.

The main bummer is that they’ll cost you more than most tees, so stocking up for the week can get pricey. Still, it’s one of those undershirts that makes you realize you’ve been settling for squalor—plus, you can bundle up and get 10% off to help offset the sticker shock.

Not everything at Uniqlo is a great value. But when it comes to upgraded basics at an affordable price, you’d be hard-pressed to find brand that does it better. When you need an airy, breathable undershirt that's truly lightweight, the Japanese mega-retailer’s AIRism tees are legendary. They’re crafted from a smooth and breathable cotton-polyester-spandex blend that dries quickly, feels cool to the touch, and fights odors—a triple threat that’ll have sweaty days in a headlock. I personally wear these—they're a failsafe way to save my expensive dress shirts from dreaded pit stains, but they’re also perfect for wearing as a gym shirt. And at just $15 per tee, there’s no other undershirt that can do as much for the price.

GQ contributor Evan Malachosky was always a little skeptical of Skims, but the brand's tees won him over. He found that Skims’s proprietary fabrics are silky on the skin, and are neither too thin (and therefore exposing), nor too thick (and therefore too hot). Pleasingly, the brand has applied just as much care to its undershirt, even though—or perhaps because—it's designed to look invisible under your clothes. (The design team even thought about cleaning up the seam lines, so nothing would show through.) Made from 100% cotton, and available in an incredibly wide range of sizes, our favorite detail is that it's a little bit longer than the brand's standard tees, so that there's no risk of any unsightly seams being visible at the hemline, either.

If the purpose of an undershirt is to fly under the radar, then it stands to reason that a V-neck one—which remains invisible even when you unbutton your shirt collar—might be the most efficient of all the styles here. You'll still want to trust the classic makers here, which is why our favorite comes from Calvin Klein. Like the Calvin Klein crewneck option above, the fabric is smooth, slightly brushed, and 100% cotton. It's also affordable, and available in not just white, black, and gray, but also a multipack comprising all three. Lastly, CK's trademark slimmer fit means no bunching or bulging risk.

Are these “undershirts” far heavier than the usual ones? Yes. But they never lose their shape, and if you live in a bitterly cold climate, you'll want even your undershirt to max out its warming properties.

The luxury car of undershirts, Falke's premium undershirts go on just as smoothly (and last just as long) as the beloved German brand's famous socks.

You heard it here first: Ralph Lauren's Pony has become the coolest label in menswear again.

When James Bond—well, Daniel Craig as James Bond—needs an undershirt, he wears Sunspel's.

Kirkland Signature is somewhat of a fashion industry secret. These are made of soft, long-staple Egyptian cotton, and they're tube knit, meaning you don't have to worry about any uncomfortable side seams.

Made from rayon and polyester, Hanes’ moisture-wicking undershirts are fast-drying, cool to the touch, and silky smooth, all for just $5 a pop.

If you wanna let your clavicles shine uninhibited by any undershirt peek-age, a V-neck is the best way (short of a tank) to do it.

Cut from a premium cotton, this lightweight undershirt is going to feel a little thicker and warmer than others on this list, purely because Reigning Champ's premium cotton fabrics tend to lean towards the beefier end of the spectrum.

Though Mack Weldon’s 18-Hour Rib Tank doesn’t come with the microbe-smashing odor technology as their Silver crew neck undershirt, it does have an even silkier fabric and plenty of stretch.

The first thing I noticed when I met Wythe's founder was not his jeans, or amazing western shirt. It was actually this ribbed tank.

Undershirts are meant to be that intermediate layer between your outermost layers and your body, a protective guard that keeps your star garments fresh and free of sweat. Therefore, it's materials, construction, and fit that are the main components that determine how good an undershirt (and, well, every garment) actually is.

Above all else, your undershirt's fabric should be breathable, soft, comfortable, and, ideally, sweat-wicking. We primarily love undershirts and tanks that are made from high-quality 100% cotton, which has many of those characteristics naturally, but we also feel like there’s a time and place for synthetics, which are often used for their ability to wick away moisture and dry easily—especially for those who run particularly hot. And note: Stretchy materials like Spandex are helpful for comfort, but their elasticity will eventually degrade over time.

Undershirts should almost always fit closer to the body than your regular T-shirts. This is because they’ll be layered underneath another shirt or sweater, and can bunch in odd ways if too baggy. They don’t need to be skin-tight, but they should be slim enough to layer comfortably and long enough to tuck into your shirt. In fact, Peter Middleton, founder of Wythe, even told us that they should fit slim to start, since they are cotton and are knit, and will therefore stretch a little over time. If they are loose to start with, they are only going to become looser and saggier, which is really not the point.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6517. Too Busy for Breakfast? Make These Pumpkin Overnight Oats

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week.

I’m not going to tell you that breakfast is the most important meal of the day. Humans have been on the planet for hundreds of thousands of years and our ability to thrive simply isn’t rooted in whether we eat first thing in the morning. In fact, the cliché is barely a century old, stemming not from nutritional science but good old-fashioned advertising.

Throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, advocates for breakfast cereal used religious rhetoric and maternal guilt to fuel their marketing efforts, while public relations executives at a pork company convinced doctors to recommend a heartier breakfast of bacon and eggs for sustained energy, aimed at working families.

Yet today breakfast is one of the most commonly skipped meals. So instead of wagging my finger at you about missing something so “important,” I think it’s worth asking: Why did you miss it in the first place?

On a jam-packed holiday like Thanksgiving, there are plenty of reasons. You have a turkey to roast. The table has to be set. Someone needs to pick up the wine. And oh, there’s still the pie dough to roll out! Maybe you even want to “save room” for the glorious feast you’re putting so much effort into.

But skipping this meal does come at a cost. Even if you aren’t ravenous, it’s metabolically valuable to eat in the morning. Breakfast stabilizes energy, and studies have shown that forgoing it leads to a reduced consumption of important nutrients like fiber, potassium, iron, and calcium, often found in morning staples like fruit, whole grains, and dairy. Without some food to start the day, you risk an energy dip, brain fog, and downright hanger. Which, let’s be honest, we don’t need in a kitchen overflowing with dirty dishes and extended relatives.

I have an easy solution. Making breakfast on Thanksgiving (or any day, really) doesn’t have to be a last-minute hassle. It can be quick to assemble and still feel special—like you’re really taking care of yourself, because you are. Take this overnight oats–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes the night before you plan to eat it.

Open up a can of pumpkin purée—odds are you bought extras that didn’t become a pie. Mix it with oats, maple syrup, and whichever milk you have in the fridge. A scoop of chia seeds adds bonus nutrition and prevents the oats from turning gluey as they hydrate overnight.

The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you. It’ll keep you full and firing on all cylinders for a day of turkey roasting, potato mashing, and vibe managing. It may not be the most important meal of the day—at least on Thanksgiving—but it will be delicious.

#6516. GTA VI Is the Most Anticipated Video Game in Human History. It Lives Up to the Hype.

There are moments in GTA 6 that’ll have you levitating off your sofa. Unprecedented in its scope and production, it was created by a team of almost 5,000 developers over nearly 10 years. Its budget is rumored to rival the construction of Dubai’s Burj Khalifa skyscraper; its first trailer set records with 93 million views in a day. Every social media brand account, from the White House to BMW, has jumped on the hype, while economists predict a national sick day as millions play hooky to game. When you do, you see the time, talent and flair on the screen. But, at its heart, Grand Theft Auto VI follows in series tradition: an epic American crime story, set in a stunning parody of the US that riffs on film, music, politics, style and satire.

Fronting the first franchise entry in more than 13 years are Jason and Lucia. Developer Rockstar attempted a multi-character arc in Grand Theft Auto V, but those three leads learned to loathe one another. Instead, VI tackles love, a game design challenge most developers have sworn off with good reason. Not a parent/child relationship like The Last of Us or God of War, but a mature, romantic, adult one. You can call or text each other at pretty much any point—to do missions together, commit robberies, explore, meditate, work out, fly, or just to coexist under the Vice City sunshine.

This isn’t some kind of ChatGPT fantasy to indulge in. Neither Jason or Lucia exists at your beck and call as some kind of hyper-realistic plaything. You have a role in their relationship, both in the way they speak to each other and where the story takes them. You can cruise down the Vice City waterfront together in your souped-up ’70s muscle wagon with one of you driving, the other scrolling through your Snapmatic feed (the in-game social media channel), before grabbing a drink and carving up the sidewalk with an assault rifle five minutes later. You just don’t get these detours in Call of Duty.

More than a car: in GTA VI, your vehicle is a mobile base of operations to stash your guns, fits, money, and drugs.

It’s a different pace from previous Grand Theft Autos too. Rockstar changed its dynamics with 2018’s Red Dead Redemption 2—a more thoughtful take on the outlaw tale that added friction to the action and a conscience to the narrative. For a developer that once experienced the spotlight of US Congress during 2005’s infamous “Hot Coffee" controversy (when a sexually explicit mini-game meant as an inside joke between developers was figured out by savvy users), this kind of nuance was revelatory. With VI, Rockstar takes Red Dead 2’s ethos and applies it to a modern city with 1,000 x the population. The result is staggering, but still an absolute blast to play. That is to say, the greatest hits of GTA—driving cars, shooting guns, and stealing money, drugs and more (all to spend on a better Beretta, G-Wagon replica, and impeccably modeled Air Jordan dupes)—but with added depth to how you play. Weapon slots are finite; you can no longer run amok with an entire arsenal stashed in your jacket pocket. Money is vulnerable; get killed or caught with cash in your possession, and you’ll lose it. And if you jack a car that’s fitted with a tracker, the police will find you quickly.

Should you get into a bust-up with the law after a jewelry store smash-and-grab gone wrong, the game’s action is frenetic. Roads are much narrower, traffic is denser, and you can’t see police on your minimap. That $40,000 in cash sitting on the back seat had better be worth the hassle. As such, the game supports your decision to play chaotically, but truly immerses you in playing methodically. Jason and Lucia each have a “criminal profile”—be unnecessarily violent and you’ll get a “psycho” rating—that adds replayability and roleplay. Still, I had the most fun when planning missions: using a silenced pistol, shooting to maim not kill, and wiping security footage to leave no trace. It’s the closest GTA has honed in on the art of crime. The feds will surround the store you’re robbing. “Come out right now with your hands above your head!” Do things right, and you’ll have prepped your partner with a getaway car out back. You’ll leave the scene anonymously as backup blares past you on the other side of the road.

Every club, pub and dingy dive bar in GTA 6’s Leonida has a distinct vibe—from the music to the decor to the sweaty Floridians inside.

The game kicks off with an electrifying setup accompanied by an original song from composers Justice. It perfectly sets the tone: VI has the ’80s flamboyance of Vice City made new and fresh. It takes its opening hours steadily, sending you on odd jobs to make a little money here and there. Gradually—then suddenly—you’re thrust into the most high-octane campaign in Grand Theft Auto history. Tense hospital escapes, daring bank heists, cross-country chases, and more. Its set pieces are balls-to-the-wall bravado, rivaling what you’d see in Nolan’s The Odyssey or Villeneuve’s Dune, upping in intensity through its chapters. Tonally, it’s the most “of the now” Grand Theft Auto game yet, as your two in-love criminals race to find a better life in an unfair world. No previous GTA has given you a savings account—it’s like playing the millennial curse. The only dings are some pacing in the game’s second chapter as the game wrestles with its story while still introducing mechanics. Think of it as VI’s version of RDR2’s Guarma, albeit with bargain bin stores and grimy strip malls instead of exotic Caribbean fauna.

And then to Leonida, with which Rockstar has created the most technically and artistically impressive game world ever made. The pre-release trailers promised beaches bustling with vacationers and nightclubs packed with dancers. That is the reality. From sea to sand to sky, the world is alive. Vice City alone could be an entire game in its own right, complete with distinct districts, an explorable international airport, and more. Yet, Rockstar spoils us with a massive expanse of varied towns, high-class beach resorts, lush green national parks, murky swamplands and sun-kissed island keys. All packed with people that range from useful, to funny, to completely unsavory (shout-out to the old woman who took one look at my Jason and said “I’mma take my teeth out and suck the skin off that dick”). The density and fidelity of it all often stretches the limits of even Sony’s PlayStation 5 Pro. Frame rate dips don’t spoil gameplay, but the slowdown is noticeable when you’ve punted a couple of grenades into passing cars to set off multiple explosions at once.

NPCs don’t just feel like backdrop mannequins anymore, but real people with an incredible range of faces, body types and outfits.

Every frame a photograph. Stop anywhere in GTA 6, and you’ll likely find something enticing to see, hear or interact with.

As with Red Dead Redemption 2, the most impressive of the game’s many achievements is how everything seems to live on without you. All it took to make this world was Rockstar founding an entire studio to work solely on Leonida’s population. I’ve seen a woman throw herself out of a cop car window as I scooted along Ocean Beach, and car thieves burst through the glass windows of a car dealership while the alarms howl. I saw a furry taken down by armed police, staged perfectly with a helicopter spotlight. During one 3 a.m. wander through the rough neighborhood of Crosstown, a man approached me to warn me of the local gang and tells me they have a nearby base. I accidentally tapped the button that brings up your in-game phone. “Ohhhh! You don’t just believe what I say” the man says, responding to my actions. “You do your own research!” In more than 70 hours of play, I have seen only one moment of repetition.

There is so much more besides. A cast of interesting, funny and believable characters; off-the-beaten-path secrets that can lead to side quests both big and small; perhaps the best radio track list of any GTA spanning from Travis Scott to Lana Del Rey; podcast episodes; golf to play; gators to hunt; dozens of supercars to steal and customize; weapons that feel punchy and satisfying; multiple racing series; a litany of actually interesting shops and bars and clubs to explore and buy things in. I’ve seen brilliant horror vignettes, startling science fiction, and laugh-out-loud comedy just by exploring. Rockstar has created a world that rewards you for spending time in it. Expect to spend 100 hours if you want to see everything.

As you’ll likely have seen and heard—in everything from Miami Heat takeovers, to Netflix launches, to Selfridges pop-ups—that this is the most-wanted entertainment property in the world. In a way, all it had to be was Grand Theft Auto V: The Second. But, on the largest and most scrutinized stage imaginable, Rockstar takes creative risks with its story, protagonists, and mechanics, and makes big leaps in what games can be. It’s unlikely other developers will catch up soon. In 2002, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City reshaped and refashioned pop culture to give us a playable version of a place and a time we already knew. A quarter of a century later, VI shows Rockstar at the peak of entertainment in its very own right.
